This paper addresses the significance of B^0_s meson lifetime measurements in identifying potential new particles with long lifespans that could explain the observed anomalies in weak force interactions involving leptons. Based on the Standard Model, the authors derive constraints on the properties of these new particles and explore implications for various beyond-Standard Model theories, including two Higgs doublet models and quark lepton flavor violation. Additionally, the researchers propose strategies to improve B^0_s meson lifetime measurements at particle accelerators and suggest new methods to reduce theoretical uncertainties.

This study aims to uncover the limitations of using classical techniques for resolving a specific stochastic control problem related to team decision-making in systems with switching dynamics and common random influences. Our findings reveal that in cases where the underlying dynamics can't handle abrupt changes, these methods fail entirely. However, our research also confirms that when applied to sufficiently smooth functions, they yield effective results. We propose an innovative approach that combines dynamic programming with the Helmholtz-decomposition theory to analyze the decomposition's components separately, ultimately finding that their combined interaction leads to successful convergence of our new method.

Our analysis of topological air shower data from the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals the direction of cosmic ray anisotropy. For particles exceeding 4 EeV in energy, we find the dipole amplitude to be 0.026 ± 0.005 (statistical) ± 0.004 (systematic) times the direction of the Lorentz boost of the Milky Way. Our measurements show the dipole amplitude seemingly increases with energy, although this apparent growth may approach the limits of our systematic precision as cosmic ray amplitudes approach fullness. We also observe a possible 2.7-sigma indication (approaching significance levels) of quadrupole structure among high-energy cosmic rays, which could become more apparent with further data analysis. With an estimated 13+/-4 events, we see a possible 2.2-sigma (less significant) indication of quadrupole structure with the same analysis restricted to energies above 24 EeV. These findings are comparable to previously reported results but with significantly improved statistical and systematic precision due to an upgrade in surface detector performance. Our findings are consistent with those from previous studies at lower energies, which revealed the deflection of incoming cosmic rays by magnetic fields.

A detailed examination of the connection between the centrality of collisions and the change in the nuclear modification factor (Rn) as a function of transverse momentum (pt) has been conducted using data from 200 GeV Au+Au and p+p runs. It was found initially that there is an evident trend where more peripheral collisions exhibit a greater variation in Rn(p t) than more central collisions, aligning with the prediction made by the CEM model for hadron production. However, this correlation does not hold true for more central collisions, particularly in p+p runs, and varies with particle type. In this investigation, we establish differential realizations of noncommutative quantum mechanics under specific conditions, where the momentum space exhibits genuine commuting properties. Corresponding to the first scenario, we derive exact energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions expressed in terms of Hermite polynomials, while the second case yields approximate energy eigenvalues via transformation to a Heisenberg algebra. Notably, our results in this study relate intimately to existing exact solutions in noncommutative quantum mechanics, featuring a linear differential structure for the Hamiltonian. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the feasibility of obtaining the standard noncommutative results as a limiting case, encompassing both one- and multi-dimensional systems, as well as incorporating the effects of linear momentum square dependence.

The detection of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes holds significant promise for the development of a non-invasive method to assess a patient's immune system's capacity to combat their cancer. Traditional techniques employed to evaluate the location of these lymphocytes within digitized tissue samples, can be slow and labor-intensive. The proposed solution involves an automated protocol based on active learning to evaluate the spatial distribution of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. This approach aims to minimize the required human effort while maintaining high analytical accuracy. By having a human expert classify a relatively small sample of training images, the associated computer model learns to identify tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. To test this method, research was conducted on three cancer samples. The results revealed that active learning could efficiently evaluate a large sample size, requiring the classification of just 0.22% of images for each analysis. Furthermore, this approach performed better than random labeling and exhibited consistent accuracy across multiple runs. The code utilized in this research is openly available for review and replication via the GitHub platform.

This paper introduces an optimized version of the List-Maximum-Sequence-Estimation (MLSE) decoding algorithm, termed as the joint decision-feedback equalization (DFE) and MLSE decoding (WDFE), specifically designed to handle burst errors in the channel. When errors occur, the adjusted metric incorporates a comparison between the primary and backup paths, allowing the algorithm to recover the original data sequence. However, when errors are isolated, a standard MLSE approach is utilized, resulting in reduced computational complexity. We develop a joint WDFE and MLSE decoding algorithm for use in long-reach optical communications systems subject to significant burst errors, caused by optical amplifiers. To evaluate its efficacy, simulations were conducted, demonstrating that the proposed algorithm delivers coding gains of up to 3.5 dB at a high bit-error rate, providing significant improvements over a conventional MLSE algorithm, while maintaining lower computational costs, while also exhibiting likely convergences to low error rates as the list size increases, while also causing the gain to decline to less than 1.5 dB, while also producing reduced errors, while yielding even more benefits, while producing significantly more gains, while also producing more than 3.5 coding gains, while producing more than 1.5 coding gains, while producing more than 3.5 coding gains, while producing more than 1.5 coding gains, while producing more than 3.5 coding gains, while producing more than 1.5 coding

Recently, highly efficient self-attention mechanisms have led to the development of efficient Transformer variants, including Recent Transformer (RC-Transformer) and Tiny Transformer Networks (TCN). Although these models demonstrate good performance, their unique architectures make fine-tuning for optimal performance challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel automatic dilation optimization method for TCNs. By leveraging the modular nature of TCN's TR units and applying a search space optimization technique, our method determines the best dilation patterns for each layer. Evaluations on the ImageNet-1K dataset demonstrate that optimally dilated TCN models achieve higher accuracy with less model size and reduced inference latency compared to non-optimized models and other efficient Transformer models. Furthermore, our method is adaptable to various inference formats, producing optimized models that outperform the original baseline models in terms of accuracy while maintaining comparable model sizes.

This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the various properties characterizing finite-dimensional algebras over a complex field, specifically focusing on nilpotency, nilpotence type, solvability, elementarity, and the dimension of the adjoint image. We achieve this by representing the algebra in its canonical basis and subsequently deriving recursive formulas for calculating nilpotence and solvability types. Additionally, we develop methods to determine the nilpotence type, nilpotency, the dimension of the adjoint image, and the upper central series of the associated Lie algebra. Furthermore, this research can be extended to algebras over any field.

According to hydrodynamic models, quark-gluon plasma flow patterns observed in fixed-angle oxygen-lead collisions mirror those in proton-lead collisions at specific momentum scales, offering a potential method to calibrate global flow measurements to elliptic flow. However, observing this equivalence is complicated by the differing geometric shapes of the collision zones and resulting initial flow fluctuations. Despite these challenges, a detailed comparison of net-particle number distributions and ratios in high-multiplicity O-Pb and p-Pb collisions reveals that, after accounting for collision geometry and flow differences, the fluctuations match for systems with similar transverse sizes and momentum ranges. Furthermore, fluctuations in more massive collisions align with those in lighter and medium-sized systems spanning from midrapidity to forward rapidity regions. This consistency supports hydrodynamic models in describing quark-gluon plasma fluctuations across a wide range of collision scenarios.

We expand upon a previous study by delving deeper into (D)LE-inductive formulas and computationally relevant aspects, with consideration for computational complexity in both non-expansive and non-contractional variants. By building on our earlier conclusion that ALBA can be adapted to handle iBCP problems associated with these formulas, we provide a more comprehensive approach that accounts for their ALBA-first order correspondents, offering a clear path to computational complexity analysis. This method offers a straightforward explanation of the relationship between (D)LE operators and their classical equivalents, and facilitates a direct derivation of ALBA-first order correspondents, enabling an assessment of computational complexity through simple, operator-based transformations.

This paper explores first-order logic within a four-valued semantics and develops a consistent query answering framework based on this framework. We propose using a specific set of theory repairs and present efficient methods to compute first-order logic queries and first-order logic formulas under these conditions. Our approach is further enhanced by showing how to determine the data complexity of arbitrary first-order logic formulas and calculating the size of its succinct representation. Our findings also have an interesting connection with the work of ten Hombergs and Van der Mey.

We introduce a novel linear dynamic statistical model, the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with exogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, which can manage complex nonlinear patterns and sudden changes in time series data with discrete outcomes. This model is effectively applied to model and forecast Twitter mentions of Apple Inc. stock, leveraging real-time data and demonstrating that the TV-PARX model's flexibility in accommodating complex, time-dependent structures makes it an ideal candidate for such applications. By transforming the time-dependent TV-PARX model into a time-homogeneous Markov process, the model's parameters can be represented as functions of its state variables, the time component from Twitter data, and exogenous variables, enabling a deeper understanding of the underlying relationships and patterns in social data.

To make manipulation tasks learned from limited demonstrations, this research
develops Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a contact state encoding neural
network that maps object contact states to contact-force descriptors. By linking
these descriptors to task performance through loss functions, NDFs can be trained
to master tasks from data collected at low demonstration rates. Our model
demonstrates success on two distinct objects with shapes that include planes,
cylinders, and curves, utilizing only 20 demonstration frames. Unlike previous
contact-state-based manipulation learning models, NDFs achieve contact stability
and transferability without relying on supervised object contact-state labels or
multiple demonstrations for each contact-state. By learning abstraction of state
contacts, NDFs use significantly less training data, exhibit stable and transferable
performance, and can adapt to new objects that have not been encountered before.

The SiD Detector is a comprehensive detection system designed for the future International Linear Collider that will allow for the precise measurement of the electrons and hadrons produced in high-energy collisions. One key component of the SiD Detector is its calorimeter system, which consists of two main parts: the central calorimeter and the forward calorimeter. Simulations of the SiD Detector's calorimeter system have demonstrated the importance of accurately modeling the material within each component, as well as any unmodeled components such as the beam pipe and vertexing system. These simulations revealed that ignoring the material system would result in a significant deviation in the calculated jet energy, particularly for high-energy jets. However, by including all material components, the calculated jet energy aligned closely with true energy levels across a wide range of energies. Additionally, the calculated velocities of these energy levels were found to be almost identical when using full material modeling, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in minimizing system-related errors.

We've analyzed the spectral features of 14 stars within the globular cluster Tononzintla 2, utilizing the VLT/FLAMES survey, and obtained precise measurements of their metallic content and elemental compositions. The results show a remarkably high metallicity for this cluster, with a very small variation in metal content, and an unusual spread in the abundance of various elements that don't follow typical patterns. Notably, Tononzintla 2 exhibits an inverse relationship between sodium and aluminum, and shows signs of previous mergers, suggesting that at least some globular clusters may contain the remnants of destroyed smaller systems. When compared to the galaxy I~Eridani~A, which also hosts stars with similar high-metallicity characteristics, Tononzintla 2 stands out as a new record-holder for the highest metal content observed in a globular cluster.

We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the formal proof archive from Proverber, focusing on metadata associated with proofs, clustering within the system's dependency network, and the scalability within the network itself. Our findings revealed that the network's node connections are determined by Proverber's node removal policy rather than Proverber's inherent content, and that the network exhibits a consistent, linear pattern in its connection clustering that can be actively managed to produce beneficial outcomes. Additionally, we observed varying scales in the distribution of node connections within specific subsets of the network that reflect the progressive increase in complexity across mathematical domains and the interconnected modular structure of modern mathematical knowledge, and the scale-free distribution of the network's overall connection pattern. Ultimately, Proverber's content serves as a foundational model for the early digital academic repositories that have not yet reached a critical mass to enable automated systems to efficiently navigate and identify emerging research trends within those repositories.

A reanalysis of the potential $V(s,\bar s)$ in QCD three-dimensions is updated and now considers the full sum over images, for both N=2 and N=4 configurations, in the large-$s$ limit. The potential's behavior at large separations is crucial for understanding the existence of a string tension in the 3D QCD, and is affected by the values of $|z_c|$, $|z_{nc}|$ and $|z_{min}|$. A new estimate for $|z_c|$ is derived and found as $z_c\sim \frac{1}{4\pi^2 s} \int_0^\infty \frac{d\theta}{Z_{eff}(\theta)}$ with $Z_{eff}(\theta) = \frac{1}{\left(1 + K_1(ks)K_0(kt) + K_1(kt)K_0(ks)\right)\left(1 + K_1(ks)K_0(kt') + K_1(kt')K_0(ks)\right)}$. This formulation is solved numerically to determine $z_c$, and it's noted that for N=4, $z_c$ increases when compared to its N=2 configuration, due to $|z_c|$ being affected by $|z_{min}|$ and $|z_{nc}|$.

We investigate the connection between the Talagancer's interpolation method and the performance of the approximate message-passing algorithm in solving $\mathbb{Z}_2$-sync. problem. Our analysis reveals that a specific convex function, derived from two-step approximate message-passing, can provide valuable insights into the same aspect of TAP free energy. For certain types of correlation matrices, this relationship between the two is even more direct. Moreover, we establish that in scenarios where the signal-to-noise ratio is significantly high, the algorithm's performance perfectly mirrors the behavior of the TAP free energy. These findings are supported by prior research and suggest that the approximate message-passing algorithm may converge to the correct solution under broader conditions than currently known.

The development of advanced metasurfaces is significantly influenced by the Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs), which undergo research and refinement to improve their application. This paper addresses the limitations of existing GSTC-based models, highlighting the need for more accurate electromagnetic modeling techniques. It Hserves as a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in GSTC research, discussing the underlying theoretical issues and Hschematics of various GSTC formulations. Furthermore, it Hschematically presents diverse applications of GSTCs in modeling thin layers, polarizing devices, and other functional components. This Hschematic review can Hserve as a starting point for researchers to delve into specific topics within GSTC-based modeling and design.

In this study, we investigate several aspects of orbital linearization for systems undergoing blowing-up transformations, specifically proving new results about immediate orbital normal forms and establishing connections between blowing-up and orbital normal forms. By establishing the concept of orbital linearization through the process of blowing-up, we create a foundation for proving a main theorem. As an application, we demonstrate the ability to achieve orbital linearization in three-dimensional systems that have a direction of symmetry and exhibit hyperbolic behavior at the origin.

We build upon our previous work to introduce an enhanced variant of the eCPNN, 
which incorporates additional hidden states to produce potential functions capable 
of accurately capturing the complex interactions between electrons across larger 
system sizes, as measured by a mean absolute error below 0.12 eV for an eight-electron helium atom. 
Furthermore, the improved model demonstrates significant generalization capabilities, 
effectively predicting ground and excited states of systems with varying nuclear charges, 
without being explicitly trained on those particular states. 
In contrast, our basic eCPNN model exhibits a notable decline in prediction accuracy 
for larger systems and is unable to represent certain electronic states due to its 
limited structural design. 
Notably, the energy potentials discovered by the improved model for both systems and the 
helium atom exhibit remarkable symmetry with respect to the coordinates of any two electrons, 
thereby underscoring the capability of eCPNN to faithfully mimic the inherently 
interwoven nature of many-body quantum systems.

We have detected a massive structure, referred to as the Giant Arc, within the cosmic web using publicly available data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Second Quadrant Redshift Survey. By analyzing galaxy distances derived from their luminosity distances, we found the Arc to be approximately 1.8 billion light-years in size, nearly three times its own height. The Arc's features are prominent in galaxy density maps and its shape doesn't align with typical large-scale structures identified in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Additionally, using matter power spectrum analysis, we found evidence of the Arc's gravitational influence on galaxy distribution, further supporting its significance. If confirmed by future surveys, the Arc's size greatly exceeds that of other large structures, including the Great Vault and the Sloan Great Wall, by more than a factor of two in width. Our findings suggest that the Arc's impact on galaxy distribution is evident in the cosmic web's overall pattern, despite the limitations of our analysis method.

This study demonstrates that extensive photometry can accurately measure the presence of atmospheric particles over a wide area, determining the optical depth of those particles to approximately 0.03. This, in turn, shows that the DUSTGRAV instrument can reliably assess the amount of dust over the Galaxia navigation panel without needing precise calibration of the device. Consequently, this discovery implies that DUSTGRAV can compare relative changes in dust levels across different areas of the Galaxia panel, using only the photometric data. As a notable example, this method successfully measured the optical depth of particles over the navigation panel, indicating that the dust layer over the panel is approximately 60 nanometers thick, which is consistent with the estimated size of the plasma screening layer. Additionally, this study indicates that the plasma screening layer's thickness can be estimated based on the scattering of light observed, as well as from independent analysis of how the light is distributed. This, in turn, provides an alternative means of controlling the plasma device used in the experiment.

Estimating object pose in scenes that include multiple instances can be a very challenging task. Existing approaches for monocular 6D pose estimation typically assume the object in question is isolated and centered in the scene. We introduce a novel, learning-based method to estimate object pose in projection points from images, allowing the system to distinguish the target object from surrounding instances and project its 3D model correctly. We modify standard 2D-CNN pose estimators by incorporating our module and demonstrate the system's effectiveness on publicly available multi-instance datasets. Notably, our method is particularly beneficial in regions that overlap with the object of interest, where projects can be very challenging. Furthermore, our method generalizes well to datasets despite each being estimated with separate models.

In this theoretical study, we model the evolution of a crack within a material that follows the peridynamic framework. The kernel's composition is broken down based on its ability to forecast the development of fractures, and an optimal kernel is identified under certain constraints. The characteristics of this kernel are also examined in simplified scenarios and compared to the dynamics of materials with short-range interactions. Furthermore, we model and contrast two types of kernels, identifying common elements between the dynamics under consideration and the Optimized Least Squares approach.

We propose G-Lasso-LV, a new model that integrates latent variables into the Graphical Lasso framework to accurately capture complex dependencies and conditional independence relationships among observed variables and an additional latent variable. This model is particularly effective in scenarios where certain critical features contribute to the correlation structure of the data but remain unobserved. Under the assumption of Gaussian distributed data, we develop an efficient coordinate-maximization-based approach for Frank-Wolfe to obtain a computationally feasible solution for general case. Our method does not rely on any sparsity assumptions, which could potentially lead to over-simplified models and inaccurate results. We also establish convergence properties of our algorithm and conduct extensive numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of G-Lasso-LV in a variety of applications, including bio-medical and social network scenarios, as well as pure regression tasks.

This study compares two popular numerical techniques for solving the Fokker-Planck
equation, specifically high-dimensional phase-space simulations of the alanine dipeptide
system. By scattering multiple processors across multiple nodes, we comically increased
our computational resources, which allowed for a more thorough analysis of the timescale
distribution. Our findings reveal that while both methods exhibit similar accuracy at
lower dimensions, the spectral method outperforms the finite difference method in
computational efficiency by up to an order of magnitude in higher dimensions. This
significant advantage translates to comparable accuracy at much lesser computational
costs.

This study explores the dynamics of binary black holes moving through a fluid environment, utilizing a theoretical model that accounts for their non-relativistic and relativistic interactions. It develops a general equation to describe the orbit's area and applies this equation to a case where the binary is surrounded by uniform, rotating matter. Two main approaches to modeling this system are presented: one assuming slow rotation and another considering rapid rotation. These approaches yield distinct formulas for the binary's orbital behavior. When the surrounding matter is present, the system's unique characteristics cause the orbit to become locked with the matter's rotation, in contrast to the case where the matter's influence is minimal, in which case the orbit's behavior is determined by initial conditions and eventually decays due to the system's radiation of energy. The results provide a framework for understanding the dynamics of binary black holes in a uniform, rotating environment and could be pertinent to systems such as the Interstellar movie scene, where a binary system orbits a large star before falling into it due to the surrounding matter's rotation.

This research investigates the dynamic behavior of a system on a star-shaped graph, where the metric of the edges changes over time in a smooth and periodic manner. We explore various elasticity conditions at the graph's endpoints, noting that elasticity is absent on the graph's internal connections. It has been proven that elasticity significantly impacts the system's exponential stability, causing it to be unattainable in most scenarios, with certain exceptions. Additionally, our study reveals that the system's long-term stability is influenced by the star's elasticity, regardless of its geometric metric. Finally, regarding elasticity absorption, we prove that the system achieves a minimal rate of stability defined by $t^\gamma u_{0} + t^{\gamma} \int |u_t|, 0\le s\le L_j, j=1,\dots, p$, where $\gamma$ varies based on elasticity dissipation on the branches.

The acoustic characteristics of two common casting materials, Stycast 1090SI and PMMA, are examined. By measuring the thickness of two materials and knowing the thickness of air, an iterative method is used to determine the properties of a mixture of materials based on its total thickness. Although Stycast 1090SI exhibits lower impedance and higher attenuation than PMMA, a material mixture can be achieved with comparable acoustic properties to PMMA. This similar material displays significantly lower attenuation, making it suitable for certain applications.

In this study, we introduce a novel method to assess the significance of nodes in multi-layer networks by incorporating betweenness centrality on each individual layer, as well as the inter-layer connections. This approach essentially expands the concept of betweenness centrality to accommodate the complex structure of multi-layer networks. Additionally, we interpret our method through the lens of shortest path calculations in multi-layer networks. To tackle the computational challenges and data limitations inherent in these calculations, we developed an efficient algorithm utilizing the shortest path trees. Our method was then applied to both artificial multi-layer networks and real-world networks consisting of social, biological, and technological layers, including a three-layer heart blood vessel network. We discovered that our method yields more differentiated results for node centrality, with distinct differences between layers, and demonstrates superior performance in identifying critical nodes in these networks.

Recent photographic trends utilize blurred areas to draw attention and create
artistic effects. Traditional methods for introducing blur involve either pre
blurring parts of an image or manipulating color and brightness to guide attention
and convey mood. We take a different approach by leveraging a camera's natural
focal inconsistencies, which vary by color, to generate focal defects that are
both image-dependent and realistic. Although these inconsistencies were once
useful for focusing, we exploit them for creative purposes by incorporating
them into image-based techniques for introducing dependency, variability, and
realism into artificial blur. We achieve this by adjusting the color and opacity
of semi-transparent focal patches, whose positions and sizes are determined by
various image characteristics, including the extent of in-camera focal inconsistencies.
In experiments, we showcase how introducing variability and unexpected areas out
of focus can make artificial blur looks more natural and less manipulative. We
also develop an method for introducing directional blur, which is influenced by
unexpected focal inconsistencies, and presents a more subtle and dynamic approach
to guiding attention in images.

The structure of the Dirac equation is derived for a spacetime called $R$-Minkowski, which has a symmetry described by the de Sitter group and can be seen as a geometric transformation of Minkowski spacetime. This derivation uses a spinor connection $\Gamma_{\mu}$ that also allows for a straightforward conversion of the Dirac equation into its equivalent form in de Sitter spacetime. Notably, the process yields a mass term in the equation, which arises due to the curvature of de Sitter spacetime, and can be reversed when converting back to $R$-Minkowski. A spinor algebra is also developed to simplify calculations involving this equation, enabling the expression of its components both in terms of de Sitter spacetime and its geometric transformation. As a result, one can easily convert between the two formulations. When applying this methodology to a free particle described by a plane wave solution, it is found that the energy and momentum measured by an observer following a geodesic path in de Sitter spacetime include a term representing the curvature of the spacetime.

We've developed the Causal Graph Modeling (CDM) framework within the R package 'cdt'. This non-Bayesian, maximum likelihood-based approach for structural equation modeling allows us to estimate the parameters of a causal graph, including path coefficients, variance, and covariance for both observed and latent variables. The implementation includes algorithms for both fully specified graph models and those requiring iterative estimation. We've used the 'cdt' framework to develop several complementary R tools, such as the 'cdtEval' package for model fit evaluation, and examples are available within these packages. Additionally, we've briefly outlined the Bayesian structural equation modeling (BSEM) model type, which combines a BSEM and CDM model, with the 'cdt' package supporting this framework through the 'htsseR' sub-package. We've also utilized the RStudio interface for enhanced usability of these packages.

This research investigates the risk of oil seal failure in rotating machinery by examining the possibility of a pressure drop that causes the seal to make contact with its surrounding surface. A model describing the seal's behavior under varying conditions has been developed, taking into consideration factors such as the seal's impact velocity, the resulting pressure reduction within the cavity, and the resulting change in cavity volume. A probability framework is proposed to assess the likelihood of seal contact with its surrounding surface, which accounts for both the average and varying components of volume change. Our derived expressions for pressure ruling out contact with the surrounding surface are verified through a case study, which demonstrates how pressure risks vary with increasing seal impact speeds. Further research in this area aims to develop more sophisticated models that capture the nuances of flow dynamics, surface roughness effects, and the statistical distributions of volume change.

Building on previous work, we explore how the G. Witten effect connects with the variety of charged states in quantum gravity through both large and minor charge disruptions. Combining the count of quantum states derived from the CFT with the principles of the Swampland, we develop a generalized formula for witten angle that encompasses the diverse charges in the theory of CFT. Furthermore, we investigate this relationship within specific SCFTs using both computation and estimation, showing that the generalized formula for witten angle can help predict the pattern of charged states across the spectrum in quantum gravity.

Mobile applications are frequently collected free of charge, yet frequently contain security vulnerabilities due to unoptimized development processes. To address this issue, we have developed OctopOS, an after-market operating system that automatically ensures the security of applications on Android devices. Built upon the Android framework, OctopOS modifies core components, including the package manager and runtime system, to insert security measures and monitor applications in real time. It can create secure access controls, enforce password policies, and generate authenticated viewing environments. Furthermore, it can enforce crypto-locked communication, apply secure data encryption, and monitor applications for malicious activities. Initial evaluations indicate that OctopOS can effectively enhance the security of applications, along with improving system performance by around 5% through the integration of performance-optimizing components.

We investigate the FPG algorithm applied to episodic controlled Markov
random walks with state space size $S$, action space size $A$, and observation
noise variance $\sigma^2$ under corrupted episodes. Under specific assumptions
regarding corruption patterns, we establish that there exists a policy learning
algorithm with a regret bound of $O\left(\frac{SC}{\sigma^2} \log T\right)$, which
linearly scales with the corruption factor and can be interpreted as an
extension of sublinear scalability seen in learning from clean data. Notably,
this is, to our knowledge, the first demonstration of guaranteed sublinear
scalability in policy learning with corrupted episodes. Moreover, we show that
without certain conditions, particularly the bounded variance assumption, no
algorithm can achieve more than $O(T)$ expected total variation distance between
estimated and optimal value functions.

A solution has been proposed to the original paradox of the "Two Envelopes Problem" using a fundamental mathematical concept - element of choice. This solution can also be applied to solve variations, or "relatives," of the paradox only under specific conditions. Those conditions involve the presence of numerically defined values within the envelopes and either a known maximum value or a specific statistical distribution. This paper seeks to illustrate why the "element of choice" cannot be utilized to resolve the original or most common formulation of the paradox, as well as certain of its relatives. Furthermore, this paper will demonstrate how applying the "element of choice" can instead, solve the original paradox of the box game.

Our first-principles investigations into the electronic and magnetic properties of cubanite and its antimonide counterpart began, building upon the discovery of this novel material by experimentalists. The starting electron count of cubanite is exceptionally high, which should theoretically lead to a unstable and disordered electronic configuration. However, the material demonstrates a robust and highly conductive electronic structure, accompanied by an easy formation of long-range magnetic ordering. Our data reveals the development of an ionic crystal lattice, with well-defined bands resembling those of free electrons filling the space between localized ion clusters. This separation of highly localized $3d$ and $5s/5p$ (or $5s$ and $3d$) electron groups is also observed in the antimonide variant, although the latter fails to achieve complete localization of the valence electron groups and displays characteristics of an electron gas filling the space between localized ion clusters. Consequently, the formation of the $21$-electron half-filled band in both compounds plays a significant role in their similar chemical stability and electrical conductivity. Moreover, the strong localization of the $4f$ electrons in the structure may provide the basis for the emergence of ferromagnetic ordering within the compounds.

By combining a quantum dot and an acoustic cavity, researchers have created a new system where the dot and cavity interact through mutual capacitance changes, thus creating an opportunity to explore and manipulate this system using a laser that targets the quantum dot while it's optically excited. Utilizing a theoretical framework, we developed a model predicting the dynamics of the quantum dot's optical properties, specifically looking at how these dynamics are affected by various factors including frequency drivers applied to the quantum dot. Our simulations showed that appropriate frequency drivers can cause regular patterns known as phonon rings around the quantum dot, and these patterns can be influenced in depth by adjusting this frequency driver, even potentially stopping the oscillations entirely. This research opens up new possibilities for developing phonon-based information systems and precise control of the quantum dot's behavior through this acoustic interaction.

A comprehensive examination of a herringbone lattice's properties is undertaken, based on the generic Hamiltonian that can be systematically altered by four parameters. These parameters are employed to linearly interpolate four distinct Hamiltonians, each representing a different physical state. By using a full-configuration interaction approach, four independent susceptibility values are calculated for each point along this interpolation path. Calculated values reveal that the herringbone lattice exists in a symmetric metallic state similar to its neighbors in the kagome and triangular lattices. However, introducing a staggered potential splits this lattice into two triangular sublattices, resulting in a semimetallic state. Further perturbation of the hopping terms induces a band collapse, leading to a band-insulating state. Ultimately, adding a three-site hopping term transforms the lattice into a semiconducting insulator. Notably, any of these lattice-breaking symmetries can be individually or combined with each other, and varying the disorder-insensitive values along the interpolation path allows for precise control over the lattice's state, resulting in a variety of phases including metallic, semimetallic, band-insulating, and semiconducting insulator states.

Researchers have successfully created highly excited states in a separate system by catalyzing coherent states in another, achieving near-maximal occupation numbers. Catalysis using a single photon on a coherent state with a 1-photon addition creates a state with 2-phons, which can be seen as an excited state with a high, but not infinite, catalytic probability. This study compares the efficiency of this process using beam splitters and parametric amplifiers, finding that the success probabilities of these methods have an interesting relationship, and as the input states' probabilities approach certain limits, they produce the same results with both beam splitters, parametric amplifiers, and catalytic processes. A look at the internal structure of the comparison equation reveals the origin of this relationship.

The Newman-Penrose formalism is utilized to represent the Weyl tensor's complex coefficients in terms of the null tetrad's complex coefficients in a general manner. This approach aligns closely with the diagonalization of a symmetric matrix, allowing us to draw parallels between the two processes. Furthermore, we examine the underlying geometric properties associated with null tetrad transformations, which facilitate the conversion from one set of coefficients to another, as evidenced by notable examples such as Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes.

Researchers have developed a new method for representing a polymer's inference distribution, based on its constituent monomers. This representation utilizes a graph neural network, specifically a Dirichlet Neural Graph Interceptor, which builds a likelihood distribution over configuration graphs that define the polymer's structure. We demonstrate through both synthetic and real-world applications that this model can effectively represent complex conditional generative tasks for a polymer without requiring assumptions about its linear structure. Additionally, it excels at representing the same flexibility as the polymer while retaining its key characteristics, such as hydrophobicity, even in challenging inference scenarios.

This study develops a novel breathing assistance system capable of ventilating multiple patients with one machine. Traditionally, each patient requires their own ventilator, but this new device uses mirror lenses to create the illusion of separate ventilators seen by each patient. Despite viewing separate images, a single ventilator controls the mirror lens system, enabling ventilation of two patients simultaneously while delivering the necessary air flow.

A widespread but challenging medical image analysis task involves segmenting the esophagus, especially when trying to accurately locate small areas like tumors within low-quality endoscopic views. To address this, we developed a modified version of the Unet architecture, called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which we evaluated on the ENDOSegInes dataset consisting of 438 esophageal images. Our model outperformed existing methods, achieving a Dice Score of 0.713 for the tumor area, and we enhanced Unet's performance by dense connections, diluted convolutions, and attention modules. Furthermore, an experimental addition of a second attention module led to improved results, and all models' performance gains were cost-effective in terms of computational resources.

Formation evaluation using a logging tool is typically done offline after the job is completed, which is too slow for real-time analysis. To address this, we've developed a novel approach called real-time multi-task learning (EnRML) on the surface of a semi-supervised loss function for the evaluation made during a logging operation. Building upon this, we've created an enhanced technique, LM-EnRML, that integrates an efficient matrix reduction technique to accelerate the evaluation. LM-EnRML allows for real-time analysis, completing the evaluation and updating the loss function in real-time. Moreover, we've incorporated an online filter to further optimize computational resources. LM-EnRML not only brings the efficiency of formation evaluation into the realm of real-time capabilities, but also significantly reduces the amount of memory required, making it applicable to an unlimited number of simultaneous tasks. We've validated our approach with over 100 concurrent tasks, where we achieved a 900% increase in processing speed and a 70% decrease in memory usage compared to existing methods.

Our research focuses on improving named entity recognition (NER) by utilizing additional context from the overall text, going beyond standard character-level features. By leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT for NER, we found that these models, while beneficial, struggle with capturing long-distance dependencies commonly found in NER tasks. To address this challenge, we developed a model called BERT-CORE, which integrates a BERT-based NER framework with a targeted information selection module. This module carefully chooses relevant corpus-level entities that aid in recognizing the current entity and can be visually presented for better interpretation. Our experiments on the OntoNotes 2.0 dataset revealed significant enhancements in NER performance with a 6.5% increase in F1-score for low-resource languages like Italian when generalization is prioritized. This performance gap is even more pronounced, reaching an 11.9% improvement, when the model's performance lags behind the base BERT NER model.

We extend a previous study by M. Saita on bitangents in the rationality class of generic quartic curves in tropical geometry. By modifying the configuration of Saita's examples, we observe that rationality of bitangents is not maintained under certain transformations. To demonstrate this, we take a specific curve from Saita's analysis, compute a non-rational set of bitangents, and provide a parametric description of this B-strand in the space of solutions.

The proposed section outlines a new algorithm for estimating the position of mobile nodes in a two-dimensional area, based on detecting their attempts to communicate with each other. A comparative analysis with other methods follows, and the method is then illustrated through simulated and real-world experiments. The results show that using pattern learning, the algorithm achieves a error rate of around 0.73 meters, which is an improvement of 27% over ideal conditions in terms of estimating mobile node locations.

Advances in natural language processing have substantially improved in value for real-world applications, such as those transforming multilingual communities, but multilingual support continues to pose significant challenges. This challenge persists despite ongoing research, particularly because current models require vast amounts of model-specific data, which is difficult to obtain at multiple languages. In contrast, pre-trained models offer a compelling alternative: they provide high-performance resources for numerous languages without the need for extensive per-language data. This work highlights the benefits and potential of using pre-trained models in the context of multilingual applications, and it explores options for selecting, fine-tuning, and leveraging such models across many languages.

A significant number of descriptions for images shared on social media platforms remain inaccurate, which is problematic particularly for users who are visually impaired and depend on technology to navigate their interactions online. Currently, there are no established standards assessing the accuracy of these descriptions, hindering the development of advanced computer systems that can translate images to text. In this context, we aim to provide a user-centered framework to create effective, priority-based instructions for enhancing the rules used in converting images to text, with the ultimate goal of refining these conversion systems. To achieve this, we gathered and analytically broke down feedback from online users, receiving responses from 543 participants who provided input based on their own experiences with text-based image descriptions. The key findings from this analysis have been incorporated into the guidelines for describing images, which can be seen in the summary below.

This study investigates local field and spin-orbit considerations in tauntalum oxide,
analyzing its computational properties and energy loss functions. Our results show the
importance of local field and spin-orbit effects for accurate computation of energy loss
functions, leading to the discovery of spin-orbit induced dipole transitions with unique
features. These results provide valuable guidance for the experimental analysis of
tauntalum oxide using techniques such as energy loss spectroscopy.

The online dissemination of unverified claims poses significant threats to society, with repercussions extending into the real world. Investigating this issue requires an understanding of how online communities organize themselves. A body of research has explored the social dynamics that influence the propagation of false information, but existing studies primarily focus on places where users from diverse backgrounds interact. In contrast, this paper examines the spread of misinformation among online communities situated in geographically isolated areas. We analyzed YouTube comments in relation to mainstream news coverage in Italy during an election period. Our findings suggest that a phenomenon known as 'The Big Sort' significantly impacts the online diffusion of unverified claims more so than other social dynamics under consideration. Additionally, this phenomenon leads to enhanced polarization, resulting in distinct political viewpoints being associated with divergent sources of online interaction. To gain a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon of 'The Big Sort', a novel metric known as The Big Sort Index was introduced. This index, along with the analysis of YouTube comments, serves as a case study for exploring the interplay between online self-segregation and political ideology.

Weakly-supervised learning has been utilized effectively in diverse fields,
including medical diagnosis, despite being able to learn from limited
annotations. This paper presents a novel deep learning technique that
combines contrastive learning and buffer learning to train models on vast
unlabeled datasets. The proposed method extracts high-quality annotations from
model predictions and refines them to exclude false positives. By leveraging
these annotations, the model is trained to make more accurate predictions,
ultimately outperforming existing weakly-supervised methods on a 20,000-x larger
unlabeled dataset. This approach demonstrates that contrastive learning can
function on massive datasets without incurring high computational costs or
expensive annotation, with practical applications demonstrated on chest X-rays
and action recognition, as code is available on GitHub.

This study aims to analyze how varying conditions impact speech learning. We A dataset called VarDemonstrations was created to facilitate this aim. VarDemonstrations is based on a dataset called Show, and it is derived from a series of teaching demonstrations given by a teacher to a student. The teaching scenarios involved in this study were recorded using screen-capture software and included both visual and auditory components. Our findings revealed significant variation in key speech content attributes across different demonstration conditions. A classification model was 93% accurate in identifying speech-learning concepts based on audio alone. While this level of variation may be acceptable in certain applications, understanding the speech learning content through speech alone is crucial, especially when designing speech recognition systems. We propose further research to better quantify and model this variation, taking into account factors such as varying levels of proficiency, age, and other related variables.

In our research, we developed a novel ordered tree reconstruction method based on the exploitation of node label properties, suitable for phylogenetic analyses. This approach allows for the inclusion of specific outdegree constraints for each node label, which are considered noninformative. We developed an efficient dynamic programming algorithm to identify all valid relabelings of a given degree matrix that align with the specified outdegree constraints, and also created a scoring method to select the most probable relabeling among the valid options. Our method was successfully demonstrated through both simulated and real data experiments, and our code is readily available for use.

Inspired by the connection between non-abelian Yang-Mills theories' flow equations and the Einstein-Hilbert action's flow, we propose an original approach to compute the non-perturbative vacuum expectation values of spatially non-local operators in QFT. This method, applicable to fields on flat Minkowski space, yields a distinct set of nonlinear differential equations for time-dependent operator functions. For fields in a flat spacetime, we show that the Euler-Arnold equations on the Grassmannian have a direct link to this approach, and certain conserved quantities for these equations, are found to be, in fact, non-perturbative values for certain physical observables. As a non-perturbative example, we consider pure gauge theory in 4D, finding that its physical observables satisfy the rigid analytic version of the Reshetikhin-Tsveik gRdger equations. This approach can be extended to time-dependent correlation functions, and we show how its discretized version leads to a gradual deformation of one metric into another, similar to the Schrodinger equation's non-perturbative formulation.

Conversational systems that are managed through chatbots are becoming increasingly dependent on robust automated testing frameworks for their effectiveness and reliability. With the numerous and intricate components of these systems, the process of quality assurance is compounded, necessitating the use of comprehensive testing frameworks to ensure they function seamlessly across multiple platforms. However, the lack of accessible and user-friendly testing tools has inhibited further progress in this area. This is particularly pronounced in the context of the Snap.2 conversational platform, where the existing testing framework is manual and cannot facilitate continuous integration/continuous deployment (CICD) processes. This work introduces an automated testing tool designed to evaluate the response outputs produced by conversational systems, allowing for the safe implementation of CICD processes. The proposed solution can be seamlessly integrated with Snap.2 and other PHP-based conversational systems, such as PHPIAA, enabling the detection of changes in natural language processing components that may affect user interactions. This tool is slated for ongoing development and can serve as the foundation for more sophisticated testing tools in the future.

We develop an iterative method to identify minimal gravity constraints on potential objects that could evade detection over large areas of the sky when using the Gaia mission for gravitational mapping. To ensure this is effective, each measurement point must take less than a minute to calculate at distances beyond one parsec. Through unsupervised clustering of these potential objects within their local neighborhoods, we refine our mass estimates for the identified sources that have significant gravitational effects near them. The approach takes approximately 10 minutes to run on one core for a sample of over a billion points, but can extract the relevant information for a given astrometric measurement with a radial extent $r_\chi$ that is taken as two times the corresponding scale length for the local neighborhood. To take account of the statistical uncertainties in the selected points, Monte Carlo simulations are used when selecting the neighborhood points. If there's no substantial disperse stellar component near the neighborhood's boundary, the boundary's radial extent can be increased to minimize measurement errors. Our method effectively identifies potential objects by analyzing the local gravitational fields near them, even when they are too faint to be seen directly. It's shown through both a flat universe and Maughan et al.'s (2021) N-body simulation with the NEU001 initial conditions that an as-yet-undetected object of similar mass to Earth would have its gravitational influence observable over more than 90% of the sky at distances greater than one parsec from the solar system.

This work explores the potential of a cross-lingual memory retriever to enhance
bilingual translation. Unlike conventional translation memory systems that
rely on exact matches between source and target sentences, our model dynamically
retrieves relevant, but potentially partial and noisy, source sentences along
with their corresponding target sentences from the translation memory. These
retrieved entries are then projected into a shared semantic space through two
separate attention-based sub-modules, allowing the model to focus on key
regions within the source sentence and the translation memory. This design
leverages the powerful TM while incorporating the valuable context provided
by the memory. Our approach demonstrates superior performance to both monolingual
translation memory and standard bilingual translation memory models on three
English-to-Chinese translation tasks, yielding a significant improvement of
1.1 BLEU points.

A theoretical prediction of cosmic inflation links the temperature of the cosmic microwave background to primordial fluctuations in density. These fluctuations, inferred from the power spectrum, should form distinct circular patterns known as "acoustic horizons" at a specific scale. Using data from the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe, researchers have found an unexpected lack of these patterns, suggesting either a problem with the standard inflationary model or an issue with current data analysis.

The inference of so-called "Hawking points" and circles with unusually low variance from WMAP data relies on using a global statistical test, which provides a reliable measure of how likely such temperature patterns are to occur naturally. However, using the likelihood ratio to identify the locations of these patterns has limitations due to the spatial distribution of these features, which can lead to biased results. A more accurate analysis using a two-point correlation function confirms that the location-based results from the likelihood ratio are generally consistent with expected outcomes, but the observed results still suggest a slightly higher probability of occurrence, although this difference is not statistically significant.

Using a Monte Carlo simulation, researchers have found that the methods used to identify these patterns do conform to the assumptions of a chi-squared test, which confirms that the lack of predicted acoustic horizons in WMAP data is not the result of statistical fluctuations in circle or variance sizes. As such, the evidence points to a potential problem with the standard inflationary model, which predicts the absence of small-scale patterns in the CMB. The

This study applies abstract y dynamics results to the Yamabe flow, yielding several key findings: Firstly, for any $\epsilon\geq0$, if the initial metric $g_0$ satisfies $\mathcal{Y}(g_0))>\mathcal{Y}(\epsilon g_{Euc})$, the constant flow $\tau\mapsto\mathcal{Y}(g_0)$ is a possible outcome. Secondly, for any $\delta >0$, if $g_0$ is sufficiently close to $\epsilon g_{Euc}$ in the $C^{4,\delta}$ norm, breaking the strict inequality $\mathcal{Y}(g_0)>\mathcal{Y}(\epsilon g_{Euc})$ prevents the existence of a smooth solution to the Yamabe flow. Thirdly, if $g_0$ meets the condition in its proximity to $\epsilon g_{Euc}$, there is a solution to the flow that grows at a polynomial rate.

Our framework for few-shot learning consists of three key components: a meta-optimizer that adapts to each new task, a filter to remove anomalous samples, and a meta-loss function based on distributional reinforcement learning.  To effectively select relevant prototypes and exclude ineffective ones, we introduce an adaptive score, oFAT-tend, that takes into account both the similarity between support and query sets and the decision margin, as well as the distribution between these sets.  Our method adapts this score using the extra information provided by the many-task training data.  Furthermore, we develop a DIggle algorithm that combines optimization and filtering to efficiently choose the most similar samples and discard the rest.  Our proposed framework addresses the challenge of anomalous data in few-shot learning, and we have confirmed its performance on the miniImageNet benchmark, showing a substantial improvement over baseline models.

User preference is an essential element in recommendation system modeling. As aspect-based preference expression becomes more common, there's a growing demand for refining the system's ability to interpret user preferences in the context of product aspects. While existing approaches have incorporated user statements and aspect features, a key limitation remains that they fail to account for user statements' inherent ability to highlight specific aspect preferences. To bridge this gap, our GAPE-Attention Profile Learning (GAPE) framework is proposed, with GAPE module focusing on enhancing the system's ability to learn user preferences in relation to specific aspects. Within this framework, GAPE Profile Learning (GAPE) is developed, with two components: first, an Gated Statement-Aspect Preference Transformation module is developed in GATE to accurately capture user preferences within given aspects, with second, an Adaptation module in GAPE used to adapt this preference representation to accommodate diverse aspect features and patterns.
