Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have significantly improved the efficiency and accuracy of time-consuming manual image segmentation, making it unnecessary for physicians to segment healthy tissue. However, the difficulty lies in training high-performing CNNs that require extensive, manually segmented datasets. This difficulty is exacerbated by the limited availability of such datasets for certain critical diagnoses. To mitigate these challenges, this paper proposes a novel semi-supervised learning framework called Boundary-Guided Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN-SLG), which utilizes boundary labels to generate pseudo masks and then conditions these pseudo masks on true labels to produce more accurate outputs. This framework is particularly effective in targeting and segmenting specific disease regions while minimizing the inclusion of healthy tissue. The model's efficacy was evaluated using three datasets with varying sizes, demonstrating its capacity to segment small regions and produce high-quality pseudo masks with minimal artifacts, as well as outperforming both full-dataset trained models and other semi-slash weakly-supervised learning CNNs.

Research on complete or nearly complete product states in four-qubit systems has highlighted the presence of nonclassical features, including hidden correlations, irreducible entanglement patterns, and nonlocal effects that cannot be classified by Bell's theorem. Nondeterministic demonstration of strong nonlocality has also been found in certain four-qubit states. Building on these findings, we have discovered that some QUBs, or UPBs, which cannot be used as entanglement resources, exhibit strong nonlocality with deterministic demonstration. This was first seen in a three-separable QUB set consisting of 20 four-qubit states, and also in a four-separable QUB set consisting of 24 four-qubit states, both of which have shown the capability to display strong nonlocality deterministically. The entanglement and correlation properties of two specific UPBs that demonstrated strong nonlocality have been investigated in detail. Moreover, we have proposed a general method for showing the strong nonlocality of four-qubit systems using four-dimensional product states. This nonlocality cannot be explained by local hidden variable theories and has practical implications for demonstrating the nonlocal behavior in multiple parties systems.

The GTOF project, consisting of three robots for optical surveys to survey thousands of optical targets nightly at the Apache Point Observatory, 6.5-meter telescope, is in full operation and collecting data. To ensure efficient and secure trajectories for these robots during this ongoing project, a approach is used for trajectory planning. A approach is used to generate and evaluate multiple possible paths, which is effective for complex scenarios but can be slow for simple situations. In order to create a robust system for real-time application, a approach combining the efficiency of quadratic programming and the reliability of collision checking is implemented. This combination includes a method for automatically generating multiple possible solutions and filtering out ineffective ones based on checking for obstacles. As a practical demonstration, this approach is tested and shown to provide optimal results quickly for multiple scenarios.

GP 2, a programming language and runtime system, is designed for parallel graph analytics on a range of systems including shared-memory computers and distributed clusters with shared storage. Recent improvements to GP 2's data handling and task management subsystems have significantly boosted its performance on such systems. Enhanced memory efficiency in BigArray, a custom data structure, allows for larger graphs to be processed without compromising performance, while reducing memory usage by up to 40% in some cases. Furthermore, performance gains observed for applications like transitive closure, shortest paths, and component identification, as well as storage accessibility features in BigFS, enable real-world applications with massive data sets. TaskQueue, a task management system, is capable of minimizing overhead and scheduling thousands of tasks per second, but also adapting to the system's available resources to maximize overall system throughput. This ensures that applications do not exceed the queue's capacity, and users are protected from submitting more tasks than their system can handle.

Our framework presents a novel, end-to-end approach to resolving either unsupervised or supervised feature extraction issues. Our approach, centered on dual learning, leverages the principles of unsupervised and supervised learning to create versatile, transferable features. Our proposed method, characterized by the use of dual learning, utilizes the uses of unsupervised and supervised learning to resolve either unsupervised or supervised feature extraction issues. Our method, centered on dual learning, leverages the uses of unsupervised and supervised learning to resolve both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction problems. Our method, centered on dual learning, makes use of both unsupervised and supervised learning to resolve either unsupervised or supervised feature extraction issues. Our method, centered on dual learning, utilizes both unsupervised and supervised learning to resolve either unsupervised or supervised feature extraction problems.

Using a combination technique, we constructed several families of infinite graphs with small non-trivial automorphism groups using a different method, further adding to a different method's successes. Our construction yields vertex-transitive graphs with primitive automorphism groups of a specific type, including A and D automorphism groups, in a systematic and efficient manner.

Lasso, a statistical tool for handling both variable selection and penalty application in continuous or categorical data, has seen various adaptations across different fields. Our development of an algorithm that combines the Group Lasso and a loss function used in survival analysis - specifically, the B-group Lasso and a Weibull model - allows for simultaneous variable selection and penalty application on distinct groups of coefficients in a survival analysis context. Our evaluation of this algorithm's performance, through simulated and real data analyses, reveals that it effectively yields a stable and efficient model, leading to accurate estimation of the original coefficients' values.

This paper investigates the connection between nonlocal diffusion models and classical PDE models. As the kernel approaches a localized limit, specific conditions are required for part of the nonlocal integral to vanish near the boundary. These conditions are essential to study the long-term behavior of solutions and establish a meaningful trace concept for nonlocal models. Our findings indicate that under this framework, the solution's decay properties and classical regularity constraints are applicable. Moreover, we demonstrate how the novel trace concept aligns with expected boundary values. Our approach is general, applicable to a wide range of kernel functions. As an example, we introduce a specific nonlocal kernel function that satisfies the required conditions and facilitates explicit computation of the decay properties and solution regularity. As a result, we derive a modified solution formula that reveals how the trace emerges from the kernel's intrinsic singularity.

Traditional panoramic stitching methods start with aligning multiple images and then proceed to detect and match features, constructing a scene map. This process can be time-consuming, especially with a large number of images. Real-time panoramic construction is challenging to achieve. Improving efficiency would significantly reduce computational costs in subsequent processing steps. In this paper, we propose leveraging inertial measurement units (IMUs) to pre-align images, enabling more efficient panoramic construction. By incorporating IMU data into the processing pipeline, we can guide the feature extraction and matching steps, creating a closed-loop system. Our method is designed to be robust against imcalibrations between cameras and IMUs, and it is demonstrated through a series of experiments using a dataset collected with a handheld device. The results show that our method outperforms traditional methods in terms of efficiency and accuracy, achieving real-time performance.

We investigate degenerate Eisenstein series associated with a non-trivial character from the Weyl group of a split simple linear algebraic group defined over the rational numbers. In the case of type A, we demonstrate that for certain cosets, these series are related to Riemann zeta functions; furthermore, we employ this property along with earlier work to establish that their special values are algebraically independent from powers of pi. Generalizing an result of Zhang, we derive formulas for the degenerate Eisenstein series of types B/C/D, linking them to local factors of L-functions and obtaining explicit results for types B2 and C2. As a result, we obtain refined independence results for the central special values of elliptic Dirichlet series and automorphic L-functions in types A, B2, C2.

How can computational models that are used for simulation and data analysis also aid in developing effective therapeutic strategies? What mechanisms can we employ to understand complex Parkinsonian states through modeling, ultimately facilitating targeted treatments? How can an agent-based model, when combined with machine learning techniques, facilitate the discovery of novel treatment approaches for Parkinson's Disease? How is a simulation-based simulation-optimization framework capable of modifying model parameters to minimize discrepancies between simulated and empirical data, F-bars values? How can this process result in the identification of new treatment ideas, such as deep brain stimulation targets and dopamine agonists? Can these ideas be validated through literature research and empirical testing? How can this cycle of analysis and experimentation refine the framework's performance? Can this cycle also lead to the identification of additional novel treatment approaches?

Recent advances in large-scale graph drawing utilize curved edges to reduce clutter and enhance visual appeal. While libraries like D3.js effectively utilize these curved edges for node connection, their handling of line joins and arrows at the endpoint proves lacking. This research introduces a novel approach to rendering fan-shaped line joins and arrows with precision. Our proposed method achieves this without resorting to complex path construction, leveraging basic line segments instead. In addition, we enhance rendering performance through the integration of WebGL, a technique we demonstrably efficient through comparative performance tests.

The recent discovery of significant outflows in galaxies, triggered by the energetic output of supermassive black holes, offers a new perspective on how galaxies and their black holes co-evolve over time. These outflows often carry away significant mass and chemical elements, which cannot be accounted for by the galaxy's own stellar feedback. Observations of active galaxies at various stages show the existence of significant outflows in both mass and chemical elements, which cannot be explained by the galaxy's own mass loss. Additionally, the velocities of these outflows suggest they play a crucial role in regulating a galaxy's evolution by influencing its cold gas supply. Galaxy mergers, which provide a powerful mechanism for channeling the galaxy's own kinetic energy into overcoming the potential barriers of both the galaxy and its black hole, offer a potential explanation for the co-evolution of these two components.

Building upon our previously introduced new radial basis function (RBF) in a preceding paper, we extend its application to create a novel quasi-interpolation formula. Despite having a large and uncountable number of degrees of freedom, this new scheme retains key properties from existing RBF-based quasi-interpolation methods developed for smooth data approximation, including variable order, derivative flexibility, and condition number flexibility. Notably, our approach preserves these variational features independently, and specifically maintains convexity and monotonicity similar to the periodic B-spline of order 2. Additionally, it is adaptable to handle both 1D and 2D data, with condition number flexibility achieved through an independent parameter, and it is capable of approximating a broad range of functions, including trigonometric, periodic, and polynomial functions.

Deep Learning methods, particularly those based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have surpassed traditional image processing algorithms and obtained remarkable results on various benchmarks.  Despite these advancements, there is still space for improvement, particularly when working with limited datasets, which is often the case in real-world applications.  To counter this challenge, we've explored two widely used data augmentation techniques cut-out and random erasing - and found their conventional applications insufficient.  By innovating beyond these methods, we aim to enhance the performance of CNNs, which rely heavily on maintaining input consistency for optimal operation.  To maintain structural information in training data, we've introduced a novel supervision function that adapts to both the output and input of the network simultaneously.  Using this, we've developed a new data augmentation method called Super Pixel Delimiting Masks (SPDMs), which combines cut-out, erasing, and mask labeling into mask pixels being set to outline the remaining pixels' boundaries as new mask labels.  By designing mask labels in this manner, SPDMs enable the network to focus on area boundaries rather than filled regions.  To further optimize mask labels generated by SPDMs, we've introduced an adaptive spacing strategy that determines mask label intervals based on object size, which helps prevent mask labels from clustering in specific areas.  By utilizing mask labels defined in this way, we've found our SPDM-based data augmentation method can enhance the performance of CNNs, particularly when training on datasets such

Speech enhancement is typically addressed through filter estimation within time-frequency domains. 
Deep learning-based methods have been successfully applied to this problem by training models to directly estimate the time-frequency filters from noisy spectral representations. 
While effective, this approach neglects the intrinsic connections between different time frames. 
To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel deep learning framework that models filter generation as a time-invariant transformation in the convolutional domain. 
Our model, called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), integrates multiple filter components learned through separate mechanisms - intrinsic dynamics captured by a convolutional neural network and error compensation learned by a separate convolutional neural network - and fuses them to produce the final filter estimates. 
Through rigorous evaluation on two widely used datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of DPCRN over dominant baseline methods in terms of speech enhancement performance. 
Our work not only confirms the efficacy of a convolution-domain learning framework but also establishes the superiority of the dual-generation mechanism with intrinsic dynamics and error compensation learning in modeling time-invariant systems.

Detailed comparisons of multfield inflation models and reheating dynamics are constrained by an extensive methodology that involves using turn-after inflation surfaces to map out potential field configurations and calculate inflationary parameters. However, before exploring complex post-inflation scenarios, it's crucial to analyze the potential field arrangements using only data from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CCT) and large-scale structures. Using a novel statistical approach, we define and calculate the turn-after inflation radii for multfield models with statistically significant differences, especially at one sigma levels, which have been shown to be distinct from each other. These differences were found to be particularly apparent, especially in the $f_R T^2$ model, where one-sigma differences in turn-after inflation radii were observed between potential field configurations. Such statistical differences, particularly in the turn-after radii, could be the key to breaking the dark sector degeneracy, especially when combined with data from the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect and the gravitational lensing of the CMB. Furthermore, our approach involves calculating the probability distributions of the turn-after inflation radii using the $\chi^2$ method, enabling us to determine if the dark matter (DM) matter could be reconciled with the data, especially in the $f_R T^2$ model, where a two-sigma difference was found in the matter power spectrum when adopting the $\Lambda$CDM values.

We develop a straightforward two-fluid model for fluid dynamics, treating fluid as composed of two intermixed components with distinct behavior but unified in the center of the velocity field. Although this approach introduces an additional length scale through its internal structure, it recovers key lengths used in analyzing turbulent motion, such as the distance where energy is transferred to smaller eddies, the distance where energy is transferred to heat, and the distance where boundaries influence energy transfer. Although the model is based on hypothetical concepts, it successfully predicts how heat transfer scales with other factors and even provides an estimate for the transfer of energy to heat based on center-line variables. Due to its simplicity, it may serve as a useful tool for understanding and designing experiments on small-scale turbulent motion within the laboratory laboratory.

We investigate the interactions between light and matter in the regime of few photons, specifically within a cavity that contains a single qubit and multiple qubits on a 1D lattice. By analyzing the entanglement within the cavity and on the lattice, we observe that moderate interactions between the qubit and cavity enhance both types of entanglement, while strong interactions diminish entanglement within the cavity but can reduce lattice entanglement as well. Notably, we find that introducing a modest amount of entanglement within the cavity has a greater potential for generating multipartite entanglement among the qubits on the lattice than does pre-existing entanglement among them. Additionally, we examine the impact of incorporating a photodetector and an ancillary atom on the entanglement within the cavity and lattice, respectively, and demonstrate that tracing out the ancillary atom can induce both types of entanglement. These findings may have far-reaching implications for the development of quantum networks.

This paper provides an overview of the silicon pixel detector upgrade for the ATLAS experiment at the LHC, which was completed in 2016. Initially, the detector consisted of 3 layers utilizing nearly 9000 silicon pixel detector modules to Atls9k a forward section and a transverse module set called AptsT1 to AptsT4. For the upgrade, nearly 4900 additional silicon pixel module modules to Atls9k were built and installed in the forward section to expand coverage and upgrade readout to two high-speed custom readout integrated circuits to nReadout. Following installation, tests at full intensity beam conditions showed that the upgrade enhanced the pixel detector performance, increasing the precision of impact parameter measurement by 15%. Also, the upgrade reduced dead areas in the forward section, improving coverage for forward muons and jets.

Using the $1/N$ expansion, we employ a numerical matrix model on a lattice to compute a pure gauge theory's glueball spectrum. For SU(2) and SU(3), with fundamental representations, we calculate a wide range of glueball masses in detail, capturing their $N$ dependence, especially the transition from the Witten limit. This approach offers a non-wedge window into QCD's strong-coupling regime.

This project aims to build an LSTM model that can effectively classify the sentiment of tweets using Python programming. Initially, we gathered a dataset consisting of 75000 Instagram comments categorized by sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral. Subsequently, we employed an Character-level LSTM architecture in Python with Keras to train the model on this dataset. Notably, our model exhibited a high accuracy rate of around 99% in correctly predicting the sentiment of tweets.

This study explores the impact of a non-linear charge parameter on theories based on Yang-Mills, using a cosmological constant and quantum corrections from D-dimensional AdS space. By applying a semi-classical approach, we examine how a non-linear charge parameter influences black holes, both in terms of their shadow radius and temperature. Our findings suggest that this parameter decreases the shadow radius and temperature of black holes, while increasing their thermal profile. Additionally, we observe a transition from stable to unstable equilibrium as the charge parameter surpasses a critical value, resulting in a collapse due to radiation pressure. Furthermore, we find that a larger quantum correction parameter leads to an increase in both the shadow radius and temperature of black holes.

Quantum state reconstruction from optical measurement outcomes is discussed with a focus on the stability of this process, particularly how the presence of classical and quantum properties are reflected in tomographic data. An examination of entanglement variability within Greenberger-Holland states reveals a direct correlation between the magnitude of variance and the nonclassical characteristics of these states, which can be further analyzed through a quasiprobability tool that accounts for the interference between overlapping signals, ultimately enabling a more nuanced comparison of the states' quantum nature.

The success of dialogue models in basic tasks relies heavily on carefully crafted guidelines. However, leveraging prior knowledge to improve real-world applications remains an unresolved issue. We make two key contributions. Firstly, we develop a flexible framework that enables the dialogue system to incorporate prior knowledge during conversations. This framework involves defining a set of rules that guide the system in formulating its statements. These statements also influence the performance of subsequent components in the dialogue pipeline. We design a efficient method for optimizing the specification that maximizes the likelihood of appropriate responses. Secondly, we focus on a practical application where we teach a chatbot to behave like a specific character. This character has unique objectives, offers advice, engages in role-playing, participates in the game, or even acts as a companion. Our approach achieves these goals by combining curriculum learning with optimal control theory. This results in enhanced role-playing performance, a useful advising assistant, a engaging game participant, and a delightful chatbot that people enjoy interacting with.

Decision support systems (DSS) have the potential to improve resource usage, disease detection, and crop yield in agriculture. To make them more useful, they need to be intuitive and user-friendly, incorporating insights from human-computer interaction, design, and psychology. However, software development methods do not typically consider how end users will interact with the system, resulting in interfaces that are often not optimized for field conditions. Furthermore, programming languages like C++ used to create high-performance software do not facilitate the integration of domain-specific knowledge, which is crucial for agricultural applications. In response, this research proposes a holistic approach that addresses the user-centered design and incorporation of domain knowledge into software development. With support from the Strawberry Yield Calculator case study, our approach demonstrates the feasibility of these ideas in a practical setting.

As 5G technology advances, high-resolution 180-degree videos are now feasible, but their streaming efficiency is hindered by the user's inability to view the entire video content simultaneously. To enhance streaming performance, adaptive bitrate techniques adjust the video quality within the user's viewing area, known as the viewport. The accuracy of the viewport prediction directly impacts streaming efficiency, leading to research efforts to develop effective machine learning models for this purpose. This research enhances these models in two key areas: first, by leveraging immersive video subtitles to provide additional contextual information, and second, by incorporating a time-series prediction sub-model to capture non-visual subtitle patterns. The results demonstrate a significant improvement of around 50 percent in prediction accuracy compared to existing approaches.

We have developed a novel constructed projected operator product state (PEPO) model that can accurately represent thermal states and time evolution for one-dimensional systems with short-range Hamiltonians, including fermionic systems in a lattice. This projected operator product state (POPS) constructively yields an efficient numerical scheme for thermal states and time evolution through its projected Hamiltonian. For a given time $t$ or thermal inverse $\beta$, the projection of the POPS results in a Hamiltonian that scales as $O(\beta)$ for large $\beta$ and accurately represents the original Hamiltonian's thermal expectation values for any $\beta \ge 1$ or fermionic systems with any $\beta$. Notably, we have demonstrated that this constructed POps model enables a more accurate approximation of thermal states than standard POps methods, particularly in the high-temperature regime. Additionally, the efficiency of one-dimensional fermionic simulations is significantly boosted, allowing us to exactly solve a fermionic chain in the thermodynamic limit at arbitrary thermal inverse $\beta$. We have also provided a link to the fermionic simulation with a non-diagonalization fermionic occupation matrix transform (FOC) and demonstrated our method's performance with time evolution and thermal expectation values for a fermionic Jordan-Chain, as well as a comparison with the exact diagonalization for small systems. All of our findings are presented in the main text, while the code for this work is hosted on GitHub.

We examine the Taylor-based decoupling concept through an exploratory framework, 
utilizing Taylor-based methods to establish a comprehensible picture of canonical 
surfaces in order to pave the way for an innovative decoupling theory. 
This is achieved initially by demonstrating the efficacy of Taylor-based 
decoupling for a specific class of canonical surfaces, 
subsequently examining a broader class within which these surfaces are included, 
and finally presenting a novel decision rule for optimal Taylor-based 
approximations as a practical tool in decoupling analyses.

This paper introduces a novel concept of anisotropic capacity corresponding to the Cheeger capacity, and demonstrates a pivotal inequality linking this concept to its counterpart, mirroring classical and recent anisotropic volumetric inequalities. Furthermore, the paper explores the representation of anisotropic capacity, as well as the continuity and concentration properties of its associated functions.

In measuring the accelerations of the PALS space experiment, glitch anomalies appear as sudden spikes in noise during otherwise smooth readings. These irregularities influence the smooth test mass acceleration measurements but their origin remains unclear, potentially stemming from various sources including laser interruptions, changes in electronic gain, or shifts in filter characteristics. By analyzing the glitches in test mass acceleration data and comparing them with the laser interruption rates, we found a strong correlation, revealing that the majority of glitches correspond directly with PALS interruptions and likely result from the closure of the photo diode filter.

We've developed a novel method to precisely control the movement of active dimers, a type of self-propelled structure, using an external force akin to a steering wheel. Our approach enables us to compare the dynamics of these active dimers to those of a rigid object in rotation and translation. To achieve this control, we created a setup consisting of a dimmer floating on a viscous fluid, which is then subjected to a unique two-dimensional flow generated by a rotating disk. This device has potential applications in teaching complex biological concepts, such as the movement of paramecia, and could also be used to explore complex swarming behaviors in simulations.

This paper explores various strong shortest path covers, including strong shortest path edge cover, ring cover, and tree cover. A particular focus is placed on the k-strong shortest path union cover problem, for which we find a strong shortest path edge cover equivalent to a 2-strong cover. Our work involves developing an $O(k|V|^k)$ algorithm for a constant k tree cover and proving the k-strong shortest path union cover problem to be NP-complete when k is greater than or equal to 3. Additionally, we present a dynamic programming solution with an runtime of $O(2^k|V|^O(k))$ for the k-strong cover problem.

Using the QCD sum rule method, we directly calculated the isoscalar and non-singlet moments of the semi-inclusive proton polarized structure function, focusing on the overlap between the proton's $u$ and $\bar{u}$ quarks. By examining the dependence on the Borel mass parameter and analyzing the competition between exponential terms, we identified possible contributions from vacuum condensates, threshold corrections, and power-suppressed terms. An analysis of the Borel plot helped us choose an optimal scale and estimate the uncertainty associated with vacuum condensates, threshold corrections, and power-suppressed terms, often referred to as "renormalons." Notably, the influence of infrared renormalons on the uncertainty estimation was found to be minimal, with a impact of only $\sim 10^{-1}$ of a unit, as the asymptotic nature of QCD perturbation theory suggests.

We investigate the relationship between a tree's structure and the frog model's behavior, specifically the point at which it shifts from transient to recurrent, in both simple and interacting versions. By examining trees with bounded degree and those with high degree, we have found that the model's behavior is directly influenced by the tree's degree. In cases where the tree has limited degree, the model's behavior remains transient for most instances, whereas in trees with higher degree, it becomes recurrent at most instances. Notably, we discovered that the model's critical threshold for its mean jump time can vary based on whether the tree's degree is limited or not. In fact, we found that if the tree's degree has certain properties, the threshold is equal to that of a randomly walking frog, whereas if the tree's degree has other properties, the threshold is higher, making it unequal to that of the random walk.

This study explores how edge states form within a specific type of boundary in a magnetized wave structure, examining these phenomena through a theoretical analysis, numerical simulations, and an experimental setup. These findings are verified by comparing them to data obtained from samples that contain different types of edges. Additionally, the magneto-optical characteristics of these samples are investigated using a specific lighting technique and a laser. It's found that the interference between surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly significantly impacts the magneto-optical spectral features of these samples, contributing to backscattering of light and the creation of an isolated state within a broader spectral range when chiral edge states meet bulk states.

We investigate decision-based knowledge distillation, or DB3, which is facilitated by black-box feedback in the form of class labels. This type of access is quite common and is made possible by numerous applications that present only classification outcomes to users, including image recognition software, spam detection programs, and even art classification tools. In contrast to traditional knowledge distillation approaches that require model outputs in the form of class probabilities, DB3 is constrained by a specific type of access and can utilize existing, high-performance models that are not easily accessible in their probability forms. Our research reveals that decision-based knowledge distillation, or DB3, is possible even with limited training data and that it can achieve considerable improvements in performance on diverse models and across different types of data. Notably, DB3 has achieved notable success in enhancing the classification performance of large deep neural networks, such as ResNet-50 and ResNet-101, which were trained on the ImageNet dataset and subsequently fine-tuned on the Pascal VOC dataset. As a result, we have produced highly effective pre-trained models that offer enhanced classification capabilities and are comparable to those obtained through more extensive training processes.

We have determined branching fractions and CP-violating phases for the decays
$B^0_{d,s} \to K^{*0}K^{*0}$ and $B^+ \to K^{*0}K^{*+}$ at a sensitivity level
exceeding five sigma for several decay modes. Uncertainties stemming from
experimental sources, branching fractions and particle masses contribute
1.6-2.6 percent, while theoretical uncertainty from isospin symmetry is
estimated between 1.1 and 1.6 percent.

Given a module $M$ within the category of $M_n(k)$-modules and its composition factors, determining the lattice of submodules of $M_c$ (where $M_c$ consists of all modules having the same composition factors as $M$) is generally not feasible. An exception to this rule occurs when the composition factors are mutually non-isomorphic. This paper addresses a more specific scenario: given $M$ with two non-isomorphic composition factors and assuming $M_c$ has two non-isomorphic submodules up to isomorphism. We derive a reconstruction formula for the lattice of submodules of $M_c$ based on the lattice of submodules of $M$. Additionally, we apply this reconstruction idea to a significant subset of modules belonging to the block of regular singular block within the category of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-modules.

The Strong Geodetic Problem involves determining if there's a subset of specified vertices in a graph that can form another subset of given vertices through the combination of shortest paths between pairs of vertices from the subset. When the shortest paths are required to be unique, the problem becomes unique shortest path geodetic recognition, and it has been proven to be NP-complete for planar graphs. However, it still remains unclear whether this problem is solvable in polynomial time for trees. This paper presents an new approach to tackle the problem, utilizing dynamic programming on a specific tree decomposition, and as a result, it develops an algorithm with a runtime of $2^\width\cdot 
pt\cdot \log 
pt$ for trees, and similarly, it also design an algorithm with a runtime of $2^ lat\cdot 
pt\cdot \log 
pt$ for more general graphs based on flatness, and these algorithms represent the first of their kind. This work, therefore, not only confirms that the problem is tractable under certain structural parameters but also these parameters can be computed efficiently in linear time for trees and approximate within a factor of $\O(\log 
pt)$ in EPTAS for more general graphs, which implies some positive aspects of this problem from an algorithmic perspective.

Imitation learning is known for reducing the need for exploration, yet it often suffers from efficiency issues as the horizon grows, typically requiring numerous samples to acquire a single piece of feedback. To overcome this constraint, we present an new algorithm named TRAIL, combining the principles of imitation learning and active learning, allowing the policy to selectively gather data where it can derive the most benefit from the teacher's preferences. In experiments on Gridworld tasks, TRAIL dramatically enhances sample efficiency in comparison to conventional imitation learning methods, achieving up to a two-order magnitude gain, and also exhibits superior sample efficiency when comparing both approaches head-to-head. We further open-sourced our implementation in PyTorch to facilitate future research.

We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a data-efficient approach that enables multiple agents to collaborate and master several tasks with only one expert's expert show. Unlike traditional co-learning methods requiring extensive demonstrations from every agent, our framework achieves performance exceeding individual learning benchmarks with a single expert's guidance. Through the combination of a communicative protocol, an adaptive data selection strategy, and a message-relevant imitation training, we facilitate effective knowledge transfer and communication among the agents. Experimental evaluations validate the efficiency and practical applicability of Co-Imitation Learning in solving complex tasks with limited data requirements.

This study examines how a decoder using the Fano algorithm and receiving a noisy sequence can effectively decision-making by selecting a appropriate polarized cutoff rate as the bias parameter. When the decoder chooses a cutoff rate that aligns with its capacity, either a finite or infinite probability of making an error becomes inevitable. In contrast, if the cutoff rate diverges from its capacity equivalent, there is a significant likelihood of a successful decision being made, resulting in a relatively low error probability. Furthermore, this research explores the impact of varying cutoff rates and their effect on the time it takes for the decoder to complete its process, both below and above its capacity equivalent. Notably, it is discovered that when the cutoff rate is significantly higher than its equivalent, there is a high probability of making an error, even if it occurs later in the decoding process.

Research by Miller indicates that reinforcement learning can produce high-quality translations from initial weak ones using iterative unwrapping techniques. Building on this, our study explores the potential of optimization in the action space, which has two key benefits: producing high-quality translations from initial weak ones and enabling efficient fine-tuning with a significant reduction in resources. Our experiments demonstrate improved performance on standard evaluation benchmarks, as well as the ability to adapt pre-unwrapped models to new languages with a minimal fine-tuning process. We further confirm our approach with additional experiments using different initialization methods, highlighting the advantages of the action space optimization in various techniques.

This research focuses on enhancing the efficiency and reliability of end-effector pose estimation, which is crucial for achieving accurate extrinsic calibration of mobile manipulators. Initially, various measurement methods are examined to determine the position of the end-effector relative to the camera. Building on this, a novel iterative optimization approach is proposed, leveraging data from both depth sensors and a rigid object model. This novel method refines the pose estimation by accounting for camera extrinsic parameters, object model, and end-effector geometry, ultimately leading to improved calibration performance. Experimental validations, including a real-time benchmark test, demonstrate the method's speed, accuracy, and durability.

This article explores the framework of QFS-spaces, which serves as a nonconstructive setting for linear logic and provides a foundation for the continuous definition of QFS-spaces. Initially introduced as a study of descent theory in topos theory, this framework offers an alternative perspective, focusing on a specific property of objects within these spaces. Key insights from this framework are clearly derivable using Python, which in turn guarantees Martin-L\"of elimination, thus avoiding any reliance on classical logic. Our analysis leads to two main conclusions regarding QFS-spaces: firstly, we establish a link between continuous retracts and QFS-spaces; secondly, we demonstrate the equivalence between QFS-spaces and spaces where double negation removal is identity, which defines a substantial subset of all types in constructive type theory. This latter finding effectively rephrases a result originally proved in cubical type theory.

The extent of hyperlinks on the World Wide Web can distort user exposure to diverse political viewpoints while they browse for information. Combined with the tendency of users to seek out content that aligns with their views, this can lead to increased political polarization. To understand this phenomenon better, we conducted large-scale tests using automated browsers across the US, Germany, and the UK. Our results show that web structures alone contribute significantly to viewing habits, causing users to encounter less diverse political views in their searches. When both factors are considered, their effects add up, pushing views encountered during browsing even further outside the user's preferred view. Developing web technologies that promote viewing diversity is seen as crucial based on these findings.

We demonstrate that the word problem for Thompson's group V can be solved using a deterministic context-free language and that any deterministic context-free language has a word problem that is equivalent to it.

We propose a method for mutual signal transmission between a quantum system and its environment. By using a device connected to a waveguide, we show that bidirectional communication is possible. This method leverages the unique features of the quantum environment to enable perfect information recovery at a distance from the original sender. Additionally, we investigate how increased information exchange rate affects the system and derive a condition maintaining the system's equilibrium. This allows us to model the impact of communication on the system. Finally, we apply our method to a practical example involving a quantum dot.

We've created a modified version of the condition for biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space that includes a broader range of cases than the original. This new definition aligns with the existing understanding of biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space and allows for a simpler, more straightforward characterization. Furthermore, it makes it easier to identify all complete finite-energy hypersurfaces within a specific type of Euclidean space. This new condition is distinct from the traditional one, yet shares similar properties. It's more flexible than the original and enables a re-examination of certain well-known results. With this new standard, we can establish the presence of complete finite-energy submanifolds within a specific type of Euclidean space that, under the original criteria, would not be considered minimal. Additionally, we can establish complete finite-energy hypersurfaces within a specific type of Euclidean space using reduced mean curvature vectors that are not normal. This new condition is not equivalent to the original one, despite sharing many similarities. It's more adaptable than the original and enables a range of re-proofs. Some key benefits of this new condition include completing the classification of complete biharmonic lines in Euclidean space, offering a more straightforward approach to the traditional formula, and providing a more straightforward approach to completing the classification of complete biharmonic hypersurfaces within a specific type of Euclidean space. An introduction to base-dependent subset recognisability in base-dependent subsets of integers based on finite-valued near-valuations with finite residues is characterised in terms of periodicity and divisibility by given numbers or their powers. Based on this, subsets of base-dependent recognisability in the rational numbers are characterised in terms of periodicity, divisibility by given numbers and their powers, as well as arithmetic progressions with common differences being powers of base numbers with sufficiently large exponents.

We examined two primary implications of the aUMSM, an SU(3) monodromy model, within the context of particle physics. To do this, we theoretically analyzed its particle content to assess the possibility of solving the strong CP problem within the model and contributing to the stabilization of the electroweak vacuum. We found that aUMSM naturally includes a heavy scalar singlet, potentially detectable through the Higgs boson's decays, and can also explain the vacua stability issue. However, in order for the model to account for the primarily observed matter in the universe, we established a minimum mass threshold for this singlet at 640 GeV. Additionally, we explored the feasibility of vacuum stability within a two-field sector of the model and mapped out the potential depths of relevant vacua. We also derived the decay rates and distances between these vacua, thereby assessing the possibility of bubbles of unstable vacua forming and colliding at the LHC. Furthermore, we determined the decay ratios of the Higgs boson into the various non-degenerate phases of the model, and if the mass of this singlet meets certain criteria, it could lead to an observable shift in the diphoton decay ratio observed during LHC operations.

Utilizing the LAMOST time-domain survey, we identified 17,844 three-season light curves, which led to the creation of a new variable star dataset known as LRVSS. By applying a specific color-cut to LAMOST data, a new binary star dataset called LRVSS was created, containing 10,876,874 binary candidates at three wavelengths. LRVSS contains stars that match certain criteria, including magnitude, exposure time, and signal-to-noise ratio, which allowed us to categorize the sample and provide a detailed description of its properties, such as a brightness distribution that peaks around 15.04 $\pm$ 0.99 lam. Additionally, we found that the BSS can account for 26.59% of the sample, and it peaks around 13.54 $\pm$ 0.99 lam. LRVSS contains some unique red blue stragglers, and we found 17 of them located within the error margins, with 12 of them located beyond the Milky Way's bulge. LRVSS contains more external objects, such as Sgr, WLM, and MagL, and we found 63 of them, including 43 of the QGRs, and 6 novae in the MagL, and 4 in the WLM. Convolutional Neural Networks, or CNNs, are versatile and highly effective for extracting features from images, but they struggle with preserving the structural and topological details necessary for accurate pixel-level predictions. To enhance the performance of CNNs in image prediction, especially in segmenting objects within images, a novel approach called Edge-Gated CNNs, or EG-CNNs, is introduced. By integrating an EG-module that learns boundary predictions and refines the flow of features through gates EG-CNNs can effectively capture object boundaries and optimize the use of spatial information within the network. The interaction between the main CNN and the EG-module creates a gentle correction that balances the details learned by the EG-module with the features learned by the CNN. As a versatile approach, EG-CNNs can be integrated into both encoder-decoder and multi-task frameworks, or used as individual heads within multi-head structures, or even as shared components for multiple task heads, depending on the specific application, or as encoder-decoder modules in combination with other EG-modules, or even as shared components for multiple task heads, or even as encoder-decoder modules in combination with other EG-modules, or even as shared components for multiple task heads, or even as encoder-decoder modules in combination with other EG-modules, or even as shared components for multiple task heads, or even as encoder-decoder modules in combination with other EG-modules, or even as shared components for multiple task heads, or even as encoder-decoder modules in combination with other

This paper introduces a practical method for verifying concurrent programs that utilize shared memory without locks, focusing on database deployments as concurrent programs. Our approach venges on Satisfiability of Concurrent Logic and extends it to check if a given database deployment satisfies specific isolation guarantees. We define and confirm that several concurrent programs do indeed meet the criteria of isolation, such as those compliant with Snapshot and Read Commit isolation standards. Our technique is particularly effective in confirming that Read Committed and other isolation guarantees are compatible with single-threaded applications. We demonstrate this by verifying the correctness of Snapshot and Read Committed isolation in the MongoDB source code, as well as the PostgreSQL single-threaded client in terms of the expected Read Committed isolation. Furthermore, we generalize our method to accommodate different specifications of isolation, such as Temporal Memory Ordering, and verify that certain database deployments do not conform to this standard. Our approach can also be used to ascertain whether a given isolation guarantee is compatible with a specific single-threaded application, and our results are open source on GitHub.

We establish that certain $e$-positivity instances of chromatic symmetric functions for Dyck paths on $n$ points, where $n$ is greater than $3$, correspond to the non-negative $f$-vector of an associated poset calculated from their down-set configurations.

We introduce a novel approach to minial learning that is guided by feedback, known as Hindsight Learning. This approach leverages "hindsight" summaries of learned lessons from prior errors to direct attention to newly attended information based on immediate feedback. Specifically, we integrate a hindsight summary mechanism—such as a RNN or FTRL optimizer—with a local attended prediction error (APRE) minimization algorithm. In this hybrid system, the hindsight module determines the attentional focus for new information, while the APE-minimizing algorithm refines a precise, localized prediction error within a small network. To efficiently store long-term lessons, the hindsight module operates economically by adjusting its parameters only at infrequent intervals. Notably, our experiments indicate that combining the hindsight module with a compact, locally optimized network yields nearly as accurate results as a significantly larger network. Furthermore, to demonstrate the versatility of our framework, we apply it to a variant of the Attention Network in Isocortex (ATIS) architecture, which models brain functions, to solve the challenging Blocks World planning problem. The enhanced ATIS system, utilizing the hindsight module, outperformed both standard gradient descent-trained ATIS and a previously proposed system that uses attention to filter attended information, even when starting with random initial conditions. The key to this improvement lies in the economical hindsight module's guided optimization of attended predictions, resulting in more precise minimization of predicted vs. actual outcomes and thus better attentional focuses.

Implicit biases in training data, often unconsciously held by creators, can
unintentionally be encoded and can unintentionally limit a model's ability to
generalize, particularly in image analysis tasks with high-stakes consequences.
We investigate how implicit biases, when present, can be learned by deep learning
algorithms and how they can differ from a model's general applicability. Leveraging
large datasets comprising millions of chest X-rays and associated patient records,
our study employs a straightforward differential privacy technique to reduce
unintentional biases while preserving useful information, with implications for
other medical imaging applications. Our findings indicate a significant decrease
in bias encoding for the COVID-19 detection model, with implicit bias
encoding dropping from 19.21% to 2.85%.

We examine the thermal behavior of a system consisting of Ising spins embedded in a simple triangular network as thermal equilibrium changes. In this network, some bond connections are specialized and involve integer variables representing up/down spin interactions, while the remaining bonds follow standard Ising model principles. Our investigation reveals that magnetic hysteresis patterns form in this network and their complexity varies depending on the fraction of specialized bonds and their internal interaction strengths. These factors influence the hysteresis loop's shape, and at certain critical points in the network parameters, abrupt changes occur, resulting in the disappearance of hysteresis patterns and further indicating signs of underlying periodic behavior.

Our study of solar interactions utilized a database of 10.5 million solar ion foams, providing insights into relationships between ion characteristics and local environmental factors at various points near the solar surface and along heliocentric paths. Comparing ion distributions near the Sun (0.32-0.95 AU) to those further away (1 AU from the Sun), we found that the F+ ion population declines as heliocentric distance increases, whereas G+ ions show the opposite behavior. Also, the energy required to escape the Sun's gravity at these closer distances exceeds that needed at 1 AU by 1.5-2 times. Both groups show the same basic pattern, with a specific threshold of sufficient energy. As ion foams approach 1 AU, the relationship between the energy and 1/r (with r being the distance from the Sun) holds up to about 0.62 AU. Our comparisons with the interplanetary shock wave data revealed that the ions often lose this relationship when caught within these waves. Also, the ion foams show signs of being turbulent as they approach the solar surface, with the G+ ions exhibiting the most chaotic behavior. Hence, the interaction between these ion groups and their surrounding plasma shows clear signs of turbulence as indicated by the calculation of the Falck number.

Emotional intelligence is considered a crucial factor in interactions with humans, and the potential to classify a person's emotional state through non-verbal cues has significant value. While some systems are capable of detecting emotions, they often struggle to generalize due to differences between training and testing data, and may also require extensive tuning. To tackle these challenges, this study presents a novel transfer learning framework based on graph neural networks, utilizing semantic graphs to enhance the recognition of emotions from text. This framework emphasizes cross-domain and cross-corpora generalization, and it enhances the classification accuracy by capturing both emotional and semantic relationships within the data. Furthermore, it introduces a compact, semantic-based model for sentiment analysis that utilizes a single, publicly available corpus to train the classifier, and then applies it to classifying emotions in diverse, previously unseen social comment datasets. The model's high performance and compactness demonstrate its ability to achieve precise emotion recognition with minimal resources, and it provides a simple, applicable solution that can be used in various domains, including web applications and mobile apps.

Research on the effects of hydrostatic pressure up to 10 GPa on Bi5FeTi3O15 under a temperature of 300 K has been conducted on a sample. X-ray diffraction was used to analyze its crystal structure both outside and inside high pressure. Results showed that Bi5FeTi3O15 possesses an orthorhombic structure belonging to the Tamura phase and that it undergoes an incompressible expansion as hydrostatic pressure increases, resulting in a phase transition at 6 GPa to a paraelectric cubical B1 structure. This transition is accompanied by the compression of the large c-axis and an abrupt reduction in the Bi5FeTi3O15 unit cell volume at the pressure threshold. Additionally, first principles calculations confirmed the experimental findings, indicating that the phase transition at 6 GPa is reversible and that an electron localization function value of 1.09 for Bi5+ and 1.37 for Fe3+ ions in Bi5FeTi3O15 in its Tamura phase.

This paper examines the discrepancies between discrete paths and optimal trajectories in systems subject to control constraints that vary over time and space, with a focus on error estimation. An infinite-length error bound formula, suitable for discrete paths, is derived under convex system assumptions. Numerical tests of a linear system demonstrate the effectiveness of a localized error bound, showing that non-parallel deviations in error bound and trajectory optimality indicate regions of possible path improvement. Furthermore, related non-parallel discrete segments are shown to have limited deviations from optimal trajectories, resulting in enhanced paths after re-computation.

When an adiabatic shock wave propagates through an homogeneous, negatively charged mass distribution, it may generate a strong singularity if a critical threshold is reached. This critical point gives rise to a singularity-free region, where the wave becomes oscillatory and produces a compact core. Our analysis shows that, for any level of adiabatic power, there is a specific threshold; when this threshold is exceeded, a singularity forms inside the wave. However, when the threshold is not reached, a compact core forms within the wave. Additionally, we have derived the internal equations governing this peculiar phenomenon.

This paper explores the connection between the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks for predicting decay rates in hadrons. By redefining the hadronic matrix elements through a specific scale, we demonstrate that both models are essentially describing the same underlying principles. By examining how different choice of scale affects the predictions, we establish a direct connection between the CLN and BGL expansion coefficients, providing a unified understanding of both frameworks.

In SUSY quantum mechanics, an infinite number of unitary transformations of the Hamiltonian, known as the polynomial Heisenberg algebra, can be utilized to explore symmetric relationships between potential energy functions and their associated spectral points. Our study reveals a connection between certain one-dimensional supersymmetric non-singular potentials and the harmonic oscillator, demonstrating that their creation and annihilation operators obey the polynomial Heisenberg algebra. Furthermore, we derive exact expressions for these operators in terms of the SUSY quantum mechanics transformation factors and Hamiltonians, and show that applying them yields the corresponding eigenstates with discrete energy levels of an infinite harmonic oscillator spectrum. Our work also establishes a polynomial algebric structure for two-dimensional SUSY harmonic oscillator by connecting it with its one-dimensional counterpart.

A new measure of disorder has been proposed for dynamical systems, based on a classic concept from physics. This measure, known as the Lyapunov dividend, is derived from average divergence and can be used to assess chaos in systems. The paper proves its applicability to various types of chaotic systems, including Lorez, R\"{o}ssler, and a new, newly discovered system. Furthermore, it establishes a connection between the Lyapunov dividend and another measure of disorder, known as entropic index, and demonstrates that the former can be calculated more efficiently than the latter.

Measurements of current-voltage characteristics in asymmetric Josephson SQUID loops have been conducted, consisting of two series-connected Josephson junctions with different dimensions. A sudden drop in switching current was observed when phase synchronization between the junctions broke, at a specific external magnetic flux value. Calculations of switching current under various models showed that the asymmetric SQUID's behavior could be represented most accurately by a two-degree of freedom hysteresis model with phase locking. In this scenario, the switching current was predicted to be two times greater than in a single Josephson junction with similar resistance-inductance values, which was confirmed by our findings. Nevertheless, phase synchronization's breakdown at a specific magnetic flux value was not supported by data. As an alternative, it was proposed that the asymptotic behavior of the central loop's Josephson current at a specific flux value might be explained by the observed behavior.

Building on previous work that added an aether term to QCD's Lagrangian, we derive a new, modified version of the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the Casimir energy based on the partition function. In the thermodynamic limit, both quantities can be expressed in terms of polylog functions. Moreover, we find that the non-abelian aether term influences these calculations in a way that mirrors its effect on the Yang-Mills path integral, ultimately allowing us to recover the original expressions when the aether term vanishes.

This research investigates the challenge of calculating the expected liquidity cost associated with a financial instrument, in this case, an exotic derivative, prior to executing a hedging strategy. The central issue lies in the fact that hedging times are interdependent, which significantly complicates the problem. To address this complication, we formulate the problem as an multiple-barrier option pricing problem and develop an efficient numerical method to solve it. The proposed solution involves a switch-ing function defined across various regions, which can be effectively computed using a refined numerical approach, specifically a radial basis function-based grid method. This enables us to calculate pre-hedging expected liquidity costs with high precision, showcasing our technique's superiority over traditional Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, the study explores various scenarios, including the calculation of optimal hedging times and the determination of optimal liquidity costs at these times. To illustrate the efficacy of our radial basis function-based grid method, the study includes numerical examples and comparative analyses with Monte Carlo simulations.

This work aims to employ variational methods to analyze an integral function that depends on both the average strain associated with linear differential constraints and the oscillation of strain in varying materials. To address this issue, we combine line of attack: compactness results, compactness theorems, and compactness properties. These approaches have potential applications in understanding linearized elasticity, electro-elasticity, and heteroclinic problems.

We utilized data from the Hubble Space Telescope's Legacy Survey of the Local Group and the Milky Way to investigate the properties of tidal structures in nearby early-type galaxies. By selecting a sample of 464 galaxies and classifying their dynamics using a multi-component model, we determined that about 9% of galaxies exhibit dynamic tails, with no significant connection to the flux fraction of tidal structures and a decreasing flux fraction as stellar mass increases, regardless of morphological type. Our findings also reveal two distinct populations in the velocity dispersion of galaxies with tails, with a higher average velocity dispersion found in one population, possibly linked to the galaxies' location in the phase diagram, regardless of their dynamical subclass. Additionally, the galaxies with tidal structures appear to be randomly distributed across the fundamental plane, with no specific preference in position.

Making decisions that benefit others in the present can have repercussions for opportunities in the future, which in turn, have different effects on various generations. This concept is evident even in simple models that account for multiple generations, as they illustrate how benefits and drawbacks can play out across different points in time, including the initial generation and subsequent ones. Given its ability to capture the multi-generational nature of decisions that affect opportunities, our framework can be used to analyze policy decisions spanning multiple periods, as well as private actions that impact future options. It also provides a structured approach to assessing the trade-offs between available options and future possibilities in both individual and regulatory contexts.

Developing and refining computer programs to simulate complex laser systems based on nitrogen-excitation and optical pumping techniques presents notable difficulties. This ambitious project, if successfully completed, would yield a highly precise simulation tool capable of mimicking the behavior of nitrogen lasers and related NLO devices. Such a device would have numerous vital applications, notably in the fields of metrology and optical coherence tomography for medical diagnostics. Nonetheless, navigating this challenge demands noting that most nlo-based systems operate in a narrow range of conditions, typically employing straightforward, compact designs. A key change has been observed recently, with several advanced systems preferring complex, multi-discharge tube configurations, often utilizing triangular or rectangular triangular forms, which in turn requires a notable modification to the underlying simulation models.

We have demonstrated that no linear operator can reduce dimensions of the ell_p unit ball (for any p not equal to 2) with isometry within a margin of error, to any one-dimensional space. Additionally, we found a specific non-linear method that maps the ell_p unit ball (with one exception) entirely isometrically into a one-dimensional space for any n-dimensional subset. We also examined related properties with scalar multiplication involved. If these optimal constants for dimension reduction by the unique non-trivial 'ell_p to ell_infinity' operators were better understood, more precise base values could be derived for various L_p spaces. We also found that the one-dimensional method based on this operator can facilitate dimension reduction of a broader class of spaces including Orlicz spaces.

The beam-beam interaction causes beams to shift at the IP in particle colliders, generating beamsqueeze and synchrobetatron coupling resonances that limit the beams' ability to collide and collide effectively. To mitigate this, the beams' paths should be corrected as much as possible. Historically, beam-beam closed orbit differences have been used to find displacement, tilt, and tripole angle of the interaction point magnets. However, these methods are limited by the beams' separation and have no direct way of identifying the tilt. We introduce new methods for calculating closed orbit differences based on the location and orientation of the IP planes that are not affected by the beams' separation. These methods can accurately determine the tilt of the IP planes using closed orbit differences measured a few hundred meters apart. Therefore, with modern accelerator layouts, the closed orbit differences can accurately measure the tilt of the IP planes, allowing for full characterization of the beam-beam interaction without needing additional diagnostics, particularly with future beamscreens in place.

This paper identifies a critical issue in distributed optimization: the vulnerability of communication efficiency when malicious agents disrupt the network as it converges to a solution. To address this, we demonstrate that non-malicious agents can maintain effective communication despite the malicious agents' interference. Our proposed stochastic gradient tracking algorithm achieves linear convergence to a optimal value on strongly convex functions over connected undirected graphs, establishing a new framework for analyzing and tracking the emergence of critical points in dynamic networks.

In the coming decade, the Simons Observatory will significantly enhance our ability to precisely measure the cosmic microwave background, by combining state-of-the-art silicon solid-state detectors and large-aperture mirrors at -40°C. While this will allow the instrument to achieve its full potential, the effects of instrumental background on its performance must be carefully considered and simulated to ensure that its full capabilities can be realized. This note aims to provide a detailed simulation of the instrumental systematic effects, including a method for predicting their influence on the data and an estimation of these effects from sample temperatures. Although this initial report does not yet incorporate time-dependent noise correlations, it does present a framework for doing so, along with specific simulations for the Simons Observatory's 95 GHz band, using 2022 data. These simulations reveal that foreground modeling, which involves accounting for the effects of foreground emissions, can be effectively used to remove the instrumental noise, by applying a weight function that down-weights data points with high sample temperatures. However, this method may not always fully compensate for the instrumental noise, by using a combination of foreground models and a variance weighting function that is derived from the power spectra of the foreground emissions. While more data and better calibration will ultimately lead to an accurate estimation of the noise, this method provides a solid foundation for refining the foreground modeling, by applying an additional model that accounts for the polarization of the foreground emissions.

Statistical barred-algebraic reordering (BART) has emerged as a promising theory for explaining the universal patterns of word order found in human languages. Despite its potential, BART's testable predictions have yet to be properly evaluated due to the absence of a computational implementation. We have created such a model, which we can train and use for evaluation. Our findings show that BART performs significantly better on word ordering tasks compared to the related partial tree linearization task. Moreover, certain aspects of our model's performance match key patterns of human developmental disorders and aging. These results validate the value of BART as a grammatical system and the efficacy of our computational simulation.

Deepfake images have countless creation methods, each with its own unique characteristics that can sometimes be exploited for detection. However, detecting them proves difficult due to various defects introduced during the fabrication process, including inconsistent textures, abnormal patterns, and compromised frequency information. To enhance detection accuracy, we introduce two innovative techniques: cross-stitch connections and region-of-interest (RoI) emphasis. Our method involves training separate detectors for natural images and Deepfake images, then connecting them with a cross-stitch connection, allowing the network to utilize prior knowledge and process current inputs effectively. Additionally, an attention-based emphasis is added to concentrate on relevant regions while down-weighting irrelevant areas, thus improving performance on multiple detection tasks using pre-trained models and demonstrating the method's superiority over existing techniques in benchmarks for Single-Image, Multi-Image, and Domain-Generalization detection.

This paper analyzes the performance of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes over erasure channels, with a focus on the impact of negative degree-degree correlation. A new, generalized LDPC graph model is proposed to facilitate the derivation of previous cutting rules and a new tolerance tolerance threshold formula. Our theoretical approach is validated through simulations, demonstrating that a negative degree-degree correlation can significantly lower the maximum tolerable erasure probability by up to 0.15. Furthermore, our new formula can accurately predict cutting rules and trends, even in scenarios where older rules are not applicable.

We analyzed the security of vacuum+weak decoy state quantum key distribution (QKD) and discovered that, contrary to single-photon attack limitations, there exists a more sophisticated photon manipulation attack feasible with currently available technology. The attack involves the eavesdropper inserting additional photon pairs into weak decoy states, making their presence undetectable while enabling key information extraction from vacuum states and one component of the photon pair's superposition state. However, measuring this superposition state triggers an error in the decoy measurement basis, which should ideally remain at low levels. If the attack is more than just a photon number splitting attack, both QKD protocols' security can be compromised, utilizing all previously utilized countermeasures. Number splitting attacks are also feasible with vacuum states, diverting them towards the trusted detector while emulating an error rate that exceeds the security threshold. Usually employed to compare keying rates between vacuum and weak decoy state QKD, the K-attack is more effective, giving the eavesdropper access to all the keying data. Although research into new attack methods promotes deeper understanding of quantum key distribution (QKD) security, we hope the photon manipulation attack's feasibility will encourage developers to enhance the security of their implementations, especially those utilizing weak decoy states.

This paper explores an energy-efficient approach for managing integrated computing and communication networks, known as edge computing. Edge computing involves strategically locating computing resources near user areas of high demand, either within central central offices or directly in nearby base stations. To reduce computing costs, we model turning off unused resources, called binarization, and potentially deactivating entire central offices, along with moving computing resource loads to neighboring stations, known as migration. Focusing on a short time period, we aim to minimize the energy used by computing resources and network equipment, while ensuring smooth operation and limited disruption. We develop an efficient method to solve this management problem by addressing the challenge of balancing load, reducing the number of migration and network equipment cases. The proposed model and reduction techniques can also be applied to optimize network equipment energy usage. Simulation results demonstrate that our strategy significantly lowers computing costs and has a minimal impact on data access delay, with migration being a more effective way to reduce energy than turning off network equipment.

This paper presents an idea from geometric analysis that has been used in various studies of conformal embeddability and related topics. Although initially applied to specific spaces, the main theorem's proof relies on principles that can be applied more broadly, offering a more general version of a concept related to angle functions. This revised understanding of the function helps determine whether certain geometric shapes can be integrated into particular spaces in a specific way.

This paper provides concrete computations related to Minkowski space. Firstly, we calculate the reduced pure type lattice for quadratic forms, then calculate the reduced pure type lattice for cubic forms, and finally give an upper bound for the minimum distance in forms in four variables.

The resolution of pressure effects on the interaction between a nitrogen jet and a surface is highly dependent on the how the jet was generated. To investigate this, two methods of nitrogen jet generation with different ways of altering jet pressure were compared. Both methods showed a shift in the location where the jet reaches its minimum cross-sectional area as the pressure changed, resulting in different shifts at both low and high pressure ranges. The research found that how the pressure was changed had a significant impact on the resolution of these effects, with two theoretical models of how the pressure change affected the jet being found to give similar results to both methods of generating the nitrogen jet.

In a young planetary system, swirling currents can break into stable, recurring patterns of motion known as self-maintained vortices.  These vortices, which form in the planar system surrounding the central star, create areas of high density in the surrounding gas and can gather and accumulate small particles, leading to the creation of large bodies, such as planets, in the system's early development.  Using computer simulations, researchers found that self-maintaining vortices can collect and accumulate small planets and contribute to the formation of larger planets and planets around a central star.  As these vortices collide and merge, their associated planets can also collide and merge, leading to the formation of larger bodies, such as moons and planets, and contributing to the system's overall growth.  Unlike other types of disturbances, which dissipate over time, these patterns of motion can persist for long periods and provide a stable environment in which small planets can gather and accumulate, and contribute to the formation of larger bodies, such as planets, and even rings around a central star, in the system's early development.  Their ability to create high-density areas and provide a stable environment, along with their ability to collect and gather small planets, and collide and merge with each other, and form spiral arms, and islands of gas, and contribute to the formation of rings and planets, and planets around a central star, and even moons, and contribute to the formation of a complex system of celestial bodies,

We develop a protocol to detect neutral modes in many-body systems that offer exceptional robustness against numerical and physical perturbations, based on slow auto-relaxation dynamics characteristic of slow dissipation. This method is effective for a broad class of open systems, including quantum systems with slow dissipation. Using many-body dynamics simulations, we demonstrate the detection of neutral modes in quantum Hall systems and semi-classically simulated rotating domains of Hall fluid. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the protocol can detect neutral modes in non-QHC (quantum Hall effect) systems and other systems lacking a neutral mode.

We demonstrate that the quantum group U_q(g) associated with a simple Lie algebra g possesses a basis bar theta with distinctive properties, particularly its compatibility with the braiding and swapping actions. This basis exhibits label invariance under the braid group's action and its closure forms a module over the quantum analog of the universal enveloping algebra of g at root unity.
